lessons.title: Escaping a loan early: prepayment penalties and a break-even you can defend
lessons.explanation: Lesson 61 established that one fixed payment conceals two different charges, interest on the outstanding balance and repayment of principal, and lesson 62 separated the stated rate from the effective rate. Both lessons assumed the schedule runs to maturity. A borrower who refinances, repays early or sells the asset that secures the loan is buying an exit, and the exit has a price that appears nowhere in the monthly payment. Three quantities price it: the payoff balance, any prepayment penalty, and the closing costs of the replacement loan. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes that a prepayment penalty typically applies only when the entire balance is repaid inside a stated window, usually three or five years, and does not normally apply to extra principal paid in small amounts, though the contract governs and state rules differ. The test is a break-even in months, computed as total upfront cost divided by the monthly payment saving. That test is valid only when the replacement loan has the same remaining term. A lower payment produced by stretching a short schedule into a longer one is mostly a longer schedule, and it will pass a naive break-even test while adding years of interest.
lessons.example: A borrower owes $268,000 at 6.75 percent with 264 monthly payments left. The payment is $1,951.32, and the remaining payments total $515,148.97, of which $247,148.97 is interest. A new lender offers 5.875 percent over 360 months and charges $5,900 of closing costs plus a 2 percent prepayment penalty, which is $5,360 on the $268,000 balance. The new balance is therefore $279,260, and the payment on 360 months at 5.875 percent is $1,651.93. The monthly saving is $299.39 and the break-even is $11,260 divided by $299.39, which is 37.6 months. The break-even looks short, but the new loan runs 96 months longer, and 360 payments of $1,651.93 total $594,694.21 against $515,148.97 for the existing schedule, which is $79,545.24 more. Now repeat the comparison over the original 264 months: the payment becomes $1,886.98, the saving falls to $64.34, and the break-even stretches to 175 months, or 14.6 years. That version does save interest, $28,246.06 over the full term, and it repays the $11,260 of cost inside the remaining life of the loan. The difference between the two answers is the term, not the rate.
lessons.question: A borrower owes $148,000 at 7.10 percent with 96 payments left, so the payment is $2,025.16. A lender offers 5.90 percent over the same 96 months, with $2,600 of closing costs and a 1.5 percent prepayment penalty, taking the new balance to $152,820 and the payment to $2,000.84. What is the honest assessment of the offer?
lessons.answer: The payment saving is $24.32 a month and the upfront cost is $4,820, so the break-even is 198.2 months, which is more than twice the 96-month term, and the cash saving over the whole term is $2,334.72 against $4,820 paid at closing
lessons.distractor: The rate falls by 1.20 percentage points on $148,000, which is $1,776 a year, so the $4,820 of cost is recovered in about 2.7 years and the refinance is clearly worth doing
lessons.correction: Applying the rate difference to the balance assumes the balance stays at $148,000 for a full year and that a rate cut converts directly into cash. It does not: the payment falls only $24.32, because the $4,820 of cost is added to the balance and repaid over 96 months, and $24.32 times 12 is $291.84 a year, not $1,776. Total interest does fall, from $46,415.66 to $39,260.70, a difference of $7,154.96, but most of that difference is the borrower repaying the $4,820 of cost inside the new balance, so the cash saving is only $2,334.72. Dividing $4,820 by $24.32 gives 198.2 months, which exceeds the 96 months available, so the borrower is behind at every point before the loan ends. This is the arithmetic that makes small-balance, short-term refinances poor value even when the rate cut looks large.

depth.definitions: A prepayment penalty is a fee payable when a borrower repays all or part of a balance ahead of the contractual schedule, usually defined as a percentage of the balance or a fixed number of months of interest, and usually limited to a stated window in consumer mortgage contracts. Closing costs are the fees charged to originate the replacement loan, including origination, appraisal, title and filing fees, and they are often financed into the new balance rather than paid in cash. The payoff balance is the amount required to settle the loan on a given date, which differs from the original principal by the principal repaid to date. The break-even in months is the upfront cost divided by the monthly payment saving, and it answers one question only: how long until the cash position improves. The remaining term is the number of scheduled payments left, and it is the constraint against which the break-even is tested. Cash saving is the difference in payments actually made; interest saving is the difference in interest charged, and the two diverge whenever the upfront cost is financed, because a financed cost is principal repaid rather than interest avoided.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that decides a refinance has three layers, and they behave differently. The payment saving scales with the balance and with the gap between the old and new rates, so it is largest when the balance is large and the rate gap is wide. The upfront cost scales with the balance through the penalty and only weakly with the balance through fixed closing fees, so small loans carry a proportionally larger cost. The break-even is the ratio of the two, which is why small balances and short remaining terms rarely clear it. The term completes the picture: holding the rate constant, every additional month added to the schedule lowers the payment and raises total interest, so a term extension can manufacture a payment saving with no economic gain. The correct procedure is to compute the saving over the existing remaining term first, and only then consider whether a longer term is worth its cost as a separate decision about cash flow. Two further refinements belong here. Interest on the replaced loan may be tax-deductible in some jurisdictions, in which case the saving should be measured after tax and the break-even lengthens. And a penalty paid now may be followed by another penalty if the borrower moves again inside the new loan's window, so the holding period has to be stated as an assumption rather than assumed away.
depth.secondExample: Take a larger balance with a longer remaining term and no penalty. A borrower owes $412,000 at 7.25 percent over 300 months, so the payment is $2,977.96 and the remaining interest is $481,389.28. The replacement loan is 6.00 percent over 300 months with $6,800 of closing costs and no penalty, so the new balance is $418,800 and the payment is $2,698.33. The saving is $279.63 a month and the break-even is $6,800 divided by $279.63, which is 24.3 months. Interest falls to $390,700.28, a saving of $90,689.00. This case clears the test comfortably because the balance is large, the rate gap is 1.25 points, the term is unchanged and there is no penalty. Compare it with the first example: a 0.875 point gap on a $268,000 balance with an 11,260 cost produced a break-even of 175 months on a like-for-like term, while a 1.25 point gap on a $412,000 balance with a 6,800 cost produced 24.3 months. The break-even moved by a factor of seven, and the rate gap moved by less than half a point. Cost as a share of balance, not the headline rate, is what separates the two.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first is comparing rates instead of payments, which treats a 1.2 point cut as a 1.2 percent pay rise. The second is comparing a new 30-year payment with an old 22-year payment and calling the difference a saving, which is a term extension wearing the costume of a refinance. The third is quoting total interest saved as though it were cash in hand, which overstates the benefit whenever the upfront cost is financed, because the financed cost shows up as principal repaid inside the new balance. A diagnostic catches all three: ask what the borrower's cumulative cash position is at month 24 and at month 60 under each option, including the cost paid at closing. If the cumulative position is worse at month 24 and the loan is likely to end before the break-even, the offer fails regardless of how attractive the rate looks. A second diagnostic is to ask which single assumption the answer depends on, and to change it: extend the holding period, raise the penalty, or shorten the remaining term, and see whether the conclusion survives.
depth.application: Build a one-page refinance test for an offer you can obtain or a realistic one you can construct. Collect five inputs: the current balance, the current rate and remaining term, the payoff quote including any penalty, the new rate and term, and the itemised closing costs. Then compute in this order. First, the current payment and the current remaining interest. Second, the new balance including costs and penalty, and the new payment over the same remaining term. Third, the monthly saving and the break-even in months. Fourth, the same calculation over the longest term offered, with the extra interest stated as a separate line so that the term extension is visible rather than hidden. Fifth, the holding period you assume, with the reason, and whether the break-even falls inside it. Complete the test when the break-even is shorter than the assumed holding period, when the same-term payment falls, and when the penalty exposure on the new loan is written down. It fails when the only saving comes from a longer term, when the penalty is omitted, or when the closing costs are described as fees rather than as principal added to the balance. This is education in loan arithmetic, not individual financial advice, and consumer mortgage rules differ by jurisdiction.
depth.summary: Price the exit before comparing rates. Add penalty and closing costs to the balance, recompute the payment over the existing remaining term, divide the upfront cost by the monthly saving, and test the result against the months you expect to hold the loan. Any saving that appears only when the term is extended is a longer schedule, not a cheaper loan.

readings.note: Read the whole answer, especially the two mechanics it states: a penalty typically applies only when the entire mortgage balance is repaid early, for example on a sale or a refinance, within a window that is usually three or five years, and penalties do not normally apply when extra principal is paid in small amounts. readings.title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan Estimate explainer
readings.note: Read the sections on the estimated total monthly payment and on estimated closing costs. The page explains that the principal and interest payment on page 1 is not the total monthly payment, because property taxes and homeowners insurance are collected through escrow, and that closing costs are the upfront charges for obtaining the loan and transferring ownership. readings.title: Federal Reserve Board, H.15 Selected Interest Rates
readings.note: Read the description of the Treasury constant maturity series: yields are interpolated by the US Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities, at fixed maturities of 1, 3 and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20 and 30 years, so a 10-year yield exists even when no bond has exactly ten years left. That is the reference structure a refinance offer is priced against. Read it for the distinction between a benchmark yield published for information and the rate a lender actually offers, which includes a spread, fees and credit pricing. The release is published daily and the values change, so use it to understand the series rather than to fix a number in a calculation.

lessons.title: When the index moves: caps, margin and the payment after a reset
lessons.explanation: The previous two lessons treated the rate as a number written into a contract and then asked what it costs to leave. An adjustable-rate loan makes the rate a formula that is re-evaluated on scheduled dates, so the payment is not fixed and the split is not fixed either. Three terms define the formula. The index is a published reference rate that the contract names. The margin is a fixed spread, stated in the contract, that the lender adds to the index. The fully indexed rate is the sum of the two, and it is the rate the borrower would pay if no cap bound. Caps then constrain the result at three levels: an initial cap limits the change at the first reset, a periodic cap limits each later change, and a lifetime cap limits the total change over the life of the loan. Because a reset recalculates a level payment over the months remaining, a rise in the rate produces a larger proportional rise in the payment than in the rate. That asymmetry is the point of the lesson, and it is the reason a household that can afford today's payment may not be able to afford the reset.
lessons.example: A borrower takes $340,000 over 360 months at 6.00 percent, with a 5/1 structure, a margin of 2.75 percent and caps of 2/2/5. The initial payment is $2,038.47. After 60 payments the balance is $316,384.81 and the remaining term is 300 months. At the first reset the index is 4.10 percent, so the fully indexed rate is 6.85 percent. The initial cap allows a move of at most two points, to 8.00 percent, and 6.85 is below that ceiling, so 6.85 percent applies. Amortising $316,384.81 over 300 months at 6.85 percent gives $2,205.96, which is $167.49 more a month, or 8.22 percent, for a rate rise of 0.85 points. At the second reset the index is 5.60 percent, so the fully indexed rate is 8.35 percent. The periodic cap allows a move to 8.85 percent and the lifetime cap allows a move to 11.00 percent, so neither binds and the payment becomes $2,515.71, which is $477.24 above the original payment, or 23.41 percent. The worst case inside the contract is the lifetime ceiling of 11.00 percent, where the payment on the same balance would be $3,100.93, which is 52.12 percent above the original. A fall in the index is not symmetric: at an index of 2.90 percent the rate would fall to 5.65 percent and the payment to $1,971.32, only 3.30 percent below the original, because the shorter remaining term works against the borrower in both directions.
lessons.question: A 5/1 loan of $240,000 started at 5.90 percent over 360 months, so the payment is $1,423.53. After 36 months the balance is $230,434.89 with 324 months left. The margin is 2.75 percent, the index at the first reset is 5.10 percent and the initial cap is 2.00 points. What rate applies and what is the new payment?
lessons.answer: The fully indexed rate is 7.85 percent, which is below the 7.90 percent initial ceiling, so 7.85 percent applies and the payment becomes $1,714.79, an increase of $291.26 or 20.46 percent
lessons.distractor: The rate resets to the 7.90 percent initial cap, because the cap is the highest rate the lender may charge at the first reset and a 3.10 point gap exceeds the two point allowance, so the payment becomes about $1,726
lessons.correction: The cap is a ceiling and it binds only when the fully indexed rate exceeds it. Here the sum is 7.85 percent, which is 0.05 points under the ceiling, so 7.85 is the rate that applies. Two further details matter. The payment is computed on the remaining 324 months and the current balance, not on the original 360 months and the original principal; recomputing over 360 months would give a payment of $1,664.40 and understate the increase. And the 20.46 percent payment increase on a 1.95 point rate rise is not an error: a level payment over 324 months is more sensitive to the rate than one over 360 months, so the payment moves about ten times as much in percentage terms as the rate moves in points.

depth.definitions: An index is a published rate, such as a Treasury constant maturity yield or a bank funding rate, named in the contract and used as the variable component; its revision frequency is specified, commonly daily, weekly or monthly. A margin is the fixed spread added to the index and is the lender's contractual return; it does not change across resets. The fully indexed rate is index plus margin. The initial adjustment cap limits the first change in rate, usually expressed in percentage points from the start rate. The periodic cap limits each subsequent change at a reset. The lifetime cap limits the total change from the start rate and is stated as a ceiling, not a schedule. A floor is a minimum rate, which may be set at the margin alone or below it, and it prevents the rate from falling even if the index does. A recast is the recalculation of the level payment over the remaining term at the new rate. A discount or teaser is a start rate below the fully indexed rate at origination, which means the first reset can move the rate without any change in the index.
depth.mechanism: At each reset the servicer performs the same four steps in order. It reads the index value specified by the contract, adds the margin, applies the periodic and lifetime ceilings, and then recalculates a level payment over the months remaining. The order matters because a contract that applies the cap to the new rate and then recalculates can produce a different payment from one that caps the change and keeps the old amortisation. Two behaviours follow from the mechanics. First, the payment is more sensitive than the rate, because the remaining term is shorter at every reset, so the same rate change moves a larger share of the balance each time. Second, the path is asymmetric when a floor exists: a falling index reduces the payment only until the floor is reached, while a rising index continues to increase it to the lifetime ceiling. Contracts also differ on whether interest-only periods are permitted, and an interest-only period followed by a reset combines two payment jumps into one date, which is where negative amortisation and payment shock concentrate.
depth.secondExample: Take a larger loan with a smaller margin. A borrower takes $520,000 over 360 months at 5.50 percent with a 5/1 structure, a margin of 2.15 percent and the same 2/2/5 caps. The payment is $2,952.50. After 60 months the balance is $480,795.14 and 300 months remain. If the index is 5.50 percent at the first reset, the fully indexed rate is 7.65 percent, but the initial cap allows only 7.50 percent, so 7.50 percent applies and the payment becomes $3,553.03, which is 20.34 percent above the original. Had the caps been written at 3/2/5, the fully indexed rate of 7.65 percent would have applied and the payment would be $3,600.08, or 21.93 percent above. The extra point of initial cap is worth $47.04 a month on this balance at the first reset. On the downside, an index of 3.20 percent gives 5.35 percent and a payment of $2,909.59, only 1.45 percent lower. The cap schedule therefore changes the first reset payment by more than a small change in balance does, which is why two offers must be compared on their caps, not only on their start rates.
depth.mistake: The four errors are using the cap as the rate, adding the margin to the note rate instead of the index, recalculating the payment over the original term rather than the remaining term, and assuming that a rate fall helps as much as a rate rise hurts. Each produces a specific wrong number: too high a payment, a rate above the ceiling, a payment too low, or an expected saving that never arrives because a floor binds. A diagnostic that exposes all four is to write the reset formula as a single line, rate equals the smaller of index plus margin and the applicable ceiling, subject to the floor, and then to check the payment against the remaining balance and remaining months. If the arithmetic cannot be reproduced from that line, the contract has a feature that has been missed, such as a discounted start rate, an interest-only period, or a cap that applies to the payment rather than the rate.
depth.application: Take an adjustable-rate offer or construct a realistic one and build a reset table with four columns: reset date, index assumption, rate after caps, and payment on the remaining balance. Populate three index scenarios: unchanged, up two points, and up to the lifetime ceiling, and compute the payment in each. Then compute the annual cash difference between the first and third scenarios and compare it with your liquid reserves; the number you want is the reserve required to absorb a full lifetime-cap reset for twelve months. Complete the table when every rate can be derived from the index plus margin rule, when each cap is labelled as initial, periodic or lifetime, and when the remaining term at each reset is stated. It fails when the cap is used as the rate, when the payment is computed on the original principal, or when the start rate is treated as the rate that will persist. This is arithmetic education, not a recommendation about any particular loan, and the index and cap conventions are contract terms that vary by jurisdiction and lender.
depth.summary: A reset applies a formula, not an opinion: index plus margin, constrained by an initial cap, a periodic cap and a lifetime ceiling, with the payment recalculated on the remaining balance and remaining months. Because the term shortens at every reset, payments move proportionally more than rates, and floors make the path asymmetric. Price the ceiling before you sign, not after the first letter arrives.

lessons.title: Lease or buy an asset: the implicit rate hidden in the rental payment
lessons.explanation: Lesson 71 priced the exit from a loan and lesson 72 priced a rate that moves. This lesson prices a choice between two ways of controlling the same asset: paying a rental for a period, or borrowing to own it. The comparison looks like a shopping decision and is actually a financing decision, because a lease payment contains a rate. That rate is implicit: it is the discount rate that makes the scheduled payments equal the asset's cash price today. Once it is extracted, the lease can be compared with any loan on the same basis, and the comparison stops depending on which total happens to look smaller. Two further adjustments are needed before the answer is trustworthy. First, the tax treatment differs: lease payments are usually deductible as an expense, while ownership brings depreciation deductions and interest deductions, and those arrive on a different schedule. Second, the cash flows must be discounted at an after-tax rate, because both options are being funded by the same business and the same tax position. A lease is not automatically cheaper because it avoids a large payment, and it is not automatically dearer because the total of the payments exceeds the price. The implicit rate, the tax timing and the residual value decide.
lessons.example: A machine costs $120,000. A lessor offers 60 monthly payments of $2,455 with no residual, so total payments are $147,300. Discounting those 60 payments back to $120,000 gives a monthly rate of 0.698 percent, which is 8.38 percent a year stated and 8.71 percent effective. The alternative is a 60-month loan at 7.50 percent, on which the payment is $2,404.55 and total payments are $144,273.23, including $24,273.23 of interest. On totals alone the loan is $3,026.77 cheaper, and the implicit rate says the same thing more usefully: the lease is priced 0.88 points above the loan. Now add tax at 25 percent. The lease payment costs $1,841.25 after tax, and discounting 60 of those at the after-tax borrowing rate of 5.625 percent gives a present value of $96,104.10. Buying means paying $120,000 and collecting depreciation deductions of $24,000, $38,400, $23,040, $13,824, $13,824 and $6,912 under five-year MACRS with the half-year convention, worth $30,000 of tax at 25 percent, with a present value of $25,726.41 at the same rate. Buying therefore has a net present cost of $94,273.59. The lease costs $1,830.51 more in present value, and the lease payment that would make the two equal is $2,408.24.
lessons.question: A business can lease a $48,000 system for 48 payments of $1,160, totalling $55,680, or borrow at 9.00 percent over 48 months, which costs $1,194.48 a month and $57,335.14 in total. What does the implicit rate say, and which option is cheaper?
lessons.answer: The payments discount to $48,000 at 7.47 percent a year, which is 1.53 points below the 9.00 percent loan, and the lease costs $1,655.14 less in total payments, so the lease is cheaper on both measures
lessons.distractor: The lease is cheaper by $1,655.14 in total payments, and its implicit rate is 9.00 percent because the equipment's market rate is set by what a bank would charge to lend against it
lessons.correction: The implicit rate is a property of the lease contract, not of the equipment market: 48 payments of $1,160 equal $48,000 today only at 7.47 percent, so the lessor is charging 1.53 points less than the bank. The total-payment comparison happens to agree here because the terms are identical at 48 months and there is no residual, but it would mislead as soon as the terms differ. A 60-month lease compared with a 48-month loan has lower payments and higher totals for reasons that have nothing to do with the rate. Extracting the rate puts both options in the same units and makes the comparison independent of term, residual and payment size, which is why it is the only version that survives a change in the offer.

depth.definitions: A lease is a contract granting the right to use an asset for a stated period in exchange for payments, with ownership remaining with the lessor unless a purchase option is exercised. The lessor owns the asset and the lessee uses it. The implicit rate is the discount rate that equates the lease payments, plus any residual value guaranteed or expected, to the asset's fair value at inception. A residual value is the assumed or contracted value of the asset at the end of the lease, and it may be guaranteed by the lessee, which transfers downside risk. An operating lease is short relative to the asset's life and leaves residual risk with the lessor; a finance lease transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership. Depreciation is the allocation of an asset's cost to periods for tax or accounting purposes, and the tax shield is the deduction multiplied by the marginal tax rate. The after-tax discount rate is the borrowing rate multiplied by one minus the tax rate, and it is the correct rate for comparing two financing options available to the same taxpayer.
depth.mechanism: The implicit rate exists because a lease is a loan in disguise: the lessor buys the asset and lends it to the lessee in exchange for a stream of payments. The lessor's required return, funding cost and view of residual value all sit inside the payment, and solving for the rate surfaces them as a single number. The tax mechanics then diverge. Lease payments are deductible when paid, so the tax benefit follows the payment schedule and is spread evenly. Ownership brings a depreciation schedule that is front-loaded under an accelerated method, so the tax benefit arrives early, and the purchase itself is not deductible. Whether the early benefit outweighs the even one depends on the discount rate and the tax rate, not on the size of the deduction: both options eventually deduct the full cost if the asset is held and then scrapped, so timing is the whole difference. Residual value cuts the other way. A lessor who expects a strong resale value can charge less, while a lessee who guarantees the residual has taken on the risk that the asset is worth less than assumed, which is a cost that does not appear in the payment.
depth.secondExample: Take a smaller asset where the answer is nearly a tie. A firm can lease equipment for $75,000 with 60 payments of $1,520, totalling $91,200, or borrow at 7.75 percent, which gives payments of $1,511.77 and a total of $90,706.20. The lease payments discount to $75,000 at 7.98 percent, so the lease is priced 0.23 points above the loan, and the total cost is $493.80 higher. Two points are worth drawing out. A rate difference of 0.23 points is inside the range that a residual assumption or a small difference in tax timing can reverse, so the decision should not be made on the rate alone at this margin. And the total-payment gap of $493.80 is 0.54 percent of the asset's price, which is smaller than the difference a single month of downtime would cost. When the two rates are this close, the decision should turn on the terms that are not in the rate: who bears the residual risk, what happens if the asset is returned early, and whether the lease bundles maintenance that would otherwise be a separate cost.
depth.mistake: The common error is comparing total payments and stopping there. Totals are only comparable when the term, the residual and the payment timing are identical, and in real offers they rarely are. The second error is ignoring tax: a lease that looks 5 percent more expensive before tax can be cheaper after tax if the business cannot use the depreciation deductions quickly, and a purchase that looks cheaper can be dearer if the deductions arrive in years when the business has no taxable profit. The third error is discounting at the pre-tax borrowing rate, which makes every future deduction look smaller and systematically favours the lease. A diagnostic that catches all three: state the implicit rate, state the after-tax discount rate, and state who bears the residual. If any of the three is missing, the comparison has not been made, only described.
depth.application: Take an asset you could plausibly acquire and build a six-line comparison. Line one: the cash price and any purchase costs. Line two: the lease payment, the number of payments, and any residual or purchase option. Line three: the implicit rate, solved from the payments and the price. Line four: the loan alternative, with its payment, term and total interest at your actual offered rate. Line five: the tax treatment of each, including the depreciation schedule for the asset class and the marginal tax rate you assume. Line six: the present value of each option at the after-tax borrowing rate, with the difference stated in currency and as a percentage of the purchase price. Complete the comparison when the implicit rate is stated, when the residual risk is assigned to a named party, and when both options are discounted at the same after-tax rate. It fails when totals are compared across different terms, when tax is ignored, or when a purchase option is treated as certain to be exercised at a price that has not been checked against a plausible resale value. Tax rules and lease classification differ by jurisdiction and change over time; the depreciation schedule used here is the US MACRS five-year table.
depth.summary: A lease payment contains a rate, and the rate is what makes the comparison possible: solve for the discount rate that equates the payments to the asset's price, compare it with the loan you could actually get, then compare the after-tax present values at one discount rate. Residual risk and tax timing decide the close cases, and totals decide nothing unless the terms are identical.

lessons.title: Invoiced in another currency: exposure, forward points and the cost of certainty
lessons.explanation: By the end of lesson 62 a loan could be described by four different rate numbers, and lesson 71 added the price of leaving one early. A contract priced in a foreign currency adds a fifth number that changes every day: the exchange rate at which the money will eventually be converted. If the invoice is in euros and the books are in dollars, the dollar amount is not fixed at the moment of sale; it is fixed at the moment of conversion, and the gap between the two dates is an exposure. Three prices are available to close that gap. The spot rate converts money now. A forward rate fixes a conversion for a stated future date and is a binding obligation for both parties. An option gives the right, but not the obligation, to convert at a stated rate and charges a premium for that right. The forward is the cheapest of the three in cash terms because it carries no optionality, and its cost is not a fee but a difference between two rates: the forward points. Those points must be expressed as a percentage of spot and then annualised, or they will be misread as either trivial or enormous. This lesson shows how to state the exposure, price the cover and compare the covered outcome with the range of uncovered outcomes.
lessons.example: A US exporter invoices a German customer EUR 1,250,000 with payment in 90 days. The spot rate is 1.0820 dollars per euro, so the invoice is worth $1,352,500 today. The 90-day forward is 1.0765, so a forward contract locks $1,345,625. The difference is $6,875, which is 0.508 percent of the spot value over 90 days. Annualising by multiplying by 365 and dividing by 90 gives 2.06 percent a year, which is the price of certainty in rate terms. The alternative is to wait. If the euro falls to 1.0510 by the payment date, the receipt is $1,313,750, which is $31,875 below the forward and $38,750 below today's spot value. If the euro rises to 1.1100, the receipt is $1,387,500, which is $41,875 above the forward. The forward therefore converts an uncertain range of roughly $1.31 million to $1.39 million into a known $1.3456 million, and it does so at a cost that is only visible when the spot rate at maturity happens to equal the forward. A third route is a put option at 1.0820 for a premium of 1.5 percent of the notional, which is $20,287.50; that premium is paid whether or not the option is used, and it preserves the upside while limiting the downside to the strike less the premium.
lessons.question: A UK exporter invoices EUR 450,000 with payment in 90 days. Spot is 1.0785 dollars per euro and the 90-day forward is 1.0730. What does the forward lock in, what does the cover cost, and what happens if the spot rate is 1.0480 at payment?
lessons.answer: The forward locks $482,850 against $485,325 at spot, a cost of $2,475 or 0.51 percent over 90 days, which annualises to about 2.07 percent, and at 1.0480 the unhedged receipt is $471,600, which is $11,250 below the forward
lessons.distractor: The forward costs 0.0055 dollars per euro, which is 0.55 percent a year, and because that is less than the exporter's 4 percent margin the cover is worth taking on cost grounds alone
lessons.correction: The 0.0055 is a difference in dollars per euro, not a percentage, and it applies to 90 days rather than a year. As a proportion of 1.0785 it is 0.51 percent for the quarter, which annualises to 2.07 percent, roughly four times the figure in the distractor. The comparison with the margin is also the wrong test. Cover is not justified because it is cheap relative to the margin; it is justified because the uncovered outcome at 1.0480 is $11,250 worse, and because the firm has budgeted at a rate it can defend. At the margin, a 2.07 percent annual cost is the price of removing a risk that would otherwise sit on the profit and loss account, and whether that price is worth paying depends on the size of the exposure relative to profit, not on the margin percentage.

depth.definitions: Transaction exposure is the risk that a known foreign currency cash flow changes in value before it is converted. Translation exposure is the accounting effect of converting foreign currency balances and results into the reporting currency. The functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which an entity operates, and for most US taxpayers it is the US dollar; amounts in other currencies must be translated into it for reporting and tax. The spot rate is the rate for immediate or near-immediate delivery. A forward rate is a contractual rate for delivery on a stated future date. Forward points are the difference between the forward and spot rates, quoted per unit of currency, and they exist because the two currencies have different interest rates. An option premium is the price paid for the right, but not the obligation, to transact at a stated rate. A natural hedge is an offsetting foreign currency cash flow in the opposite direction, such as costs incurred in the same currency as revenue.
depth.mechanism: Forward points are not a fee charged by a bank; they are the market's way of equalising the return from holding two currencies over the same period. If one currency offers a higher interest rate, a forward contract that lets an investor hold the other currency must be priced so that the interest advantage is offset, which is covered interest parity. The practical consequence is that a forward at a discount signals that the foreign currency interest rate is lower than the domestic one over that period, and a forward at a premium signals the reverse. This is why forward points are predictable from interest rates and why they are not a forecast of the spot rate. Second, a forward is binding: it removes downside and upside together, unlike an option, which removes downside and keeps upside for a premium. Third, the exposure can be shifted by the contract itself: invoicing in the customer's currency transfers the risk to the seller, invoicing in the seller's currency transfers it to the buyer, and pricing will usually adjust to reflect who carries it. The accounting and tax treatment then follows the functional currency, not the invoice currency.
depth.secondExample: Take a euro receivable with a longer horizon. A firm expects EUR 480,000 in 180 days. Spot is 1.0845, so the exposure is $520,560, and the 180-day forward is 1.0790, locking $517,920. The cost of cover is $2,640, which is 0.507 percent over 180 days and 1.03 percent annualised, lower than the 90-day case in rate terms because the annualisation spreads a similar percentage over twice the period. If the euro falls 3 percent to 1.0520, the unhedged receipt is $504,960, which is $12,960 below the forward, and the gap is 2.5 percent of the hedged value. If the euro rises 3 percent to 1.1171, the unhedged receipt is $536,208, which is $18,288 above the forward. The asymmetry in those two numbers, 12,960 down and 18,288 up, is not a market judgement; it follows from applying the same 3 percent move to a rate that is slightly below spot. Cover is a decision about which of those two outcomes the business can survive, not a bet on which is more likely.
depth.mistake: Reading forward points as a percentage when they are a currency amount per unit is the first error, and it understates a quarterly cost by a factor of 100 and an annual cost by more. Annualising with the wrong day count, usually 360 days when the contract quotes 365, is the second, though it is small compared with failing to annualise at all. The third is comparing the forward rate with the spot rate on the day the contract was signed and concluding that the forward was a loss or a gain, when the relevant comparison is with the spot rate on the day the money would have been converted. A forward that locks 1.0765 against a spot of 1.0820 has not lost 0.0055; it has bought certainty for 0.508 percent of the exposure, and the outcome is judged against what the spot rate actually did. A diagnostic: write the exposure, the hedged outcome, the unhedged outcome at two spot scenarios and the cost of cover as a percentage of exposure, and check that all four numbers are in the same units.
depth.application: Build a currency exposure table for a contract you can realistically imagine or one you are involved in. Columns: invoice amount and currency, payment date, functional currency, spot rate on the invoice date, the dollar value at spot, the forward rate for the payment date, the hedged dollar value, and the difference in dollars and as a percentage of exposure. Then add three spot scenarios for the payment date, a fall of 3 percent, unchanged, and a rise of 3 percent, and compute the unhedged receipt in each. Complete the table when the cost of cover is annualised, when the worst unhedged outcome is compared with the profit the contract is expected to earn, and when a decision rule is written down, for example cover whenever the unhedged worst case exceeds a stated share of expected profit. It fails when forward points are quoted as a percentage without conversion, when the forward is compared with spot at inception rather than at maturity, or when the hedge is described as free. Exchange rate conventions, day counts and tax translation rules differ by jurisdiction; the tax treatment described here follows US rules for a dollar functional currency.
depth.summary: An invoice in another currency is two transactions: a sale and a currency conversion at an unknown future rate. State the exposure, price the forward as a percentage of spot and annualise it, compare the hedged outcome with the range of unhedged outcomes, and decide which range the business can absorb. Forward points are an interest differential, not a fee, and they are not a forecast.

lessons.title: Guarantees and contingent liabilities: the loss you owe when someone else defaults
lessons.explanation: Lesson 65 established that ratios measure rather than judge, and lessons 71 and 72 showed how a loan's terms change its cost. A personal or corporate guarantee adds a liability that appears in none of those measures until it is called. The guarantor has promised to pay someone else's debt if the borrower does not, so the obligation is contingent: there is no cash outflow in the ordinary case and a large one in the bad case. Three quantities price it. Exposure is the amount guaranteed, which may be the full balance or a stated percentage. The probability of default is the chance the primary borrower fails to pay over a stated period. The loss given default is the share of the exposure that is not recovered, which is one minus the recovery rate. Expected loss is the product of the three, and it is the number an insurer would charge for carrying the risk. It is not the number that constrains the guarantor. The constraint is the cash call in the bad state and its effect on coverage, because a guarantee that is called converts a contingent obligation into a fixed charge, and lenders count the full exposure when they assess the guarantor's capacity.
lessons.example: A business owner guarantees 80 percent of a $250,000 loan, so the exposure is $200,000. The lender's experience suggests a 4 percent annual probability of default and 35 percent recovery on defaulted small business loans, so the loss given default is 65 percent. Expected loss is $250,000 multiplied by 0.80, multiplied by 0.04, multiplied by 0.65, which is $5,200 a year. That figure is small relative to the owner's $96,000 of income, and it is the wrong number to plan around. If the guarantee is called, the owner owes the $200,000, and servicing it at 9 percent interest-only costs $18,000 a year. Add the $9,000 of existing personal debt service and the total is $27,000, or 28.1 percent of gross income, before any principal repayment. A lender assessing the owner's next mortgage would count the full $200,000 as a contingent liability and would likely treat the debt service coverage as breached at that level. The gap between $5,200 and $18,000 is the gap between a probability-weighted cost and a cash obligation, and both are needed: the first prices the risk, the second sizes the damage.
lessons.question: A director guarantees 90 percent of a $180,000 facility. The lender assumes a 3.5 percent annual default probability and 30 percent recovery. What is the expected loss, and what annual interest would the director owe if the guarantee were called at 8 percent?
lessons.answer: Exposure is $162,000, loss given default is 70 percent, expected loss is $3,969 a year, and a call would cost $12,960 a year in interest at 8 percent, which is 13.5 percent of $96,000 of income
lessons.distractor: Expected loss is $6,300 because 3.5 percent of $180,000 is $6,300, and the guarantee is a disclosure item rather than a liability because the company is currently paying on time
lessons.correction: The $6,300 uses the full facility and ignores both the 90 percent guarantee and the 30 percent recovery. The correct exposure is $162,000, the unrecovered share is 70 percent, and 3.5 percent of $113,400 is $3,969. The second error is larger. A guarantee is not a disclosure item: the lender can call it without waiting for the company to fail completely, and in a workout it becomes a demand on the director's own assets. The annual cost in the bad state is $12,960, and that is the figure that should be compared with the director's other commitments. The expected loss is the right number for pricing the risk and the wrong number for deciding whether the risk can be borne.

depth.definitions: A guarantee is a promise by one party to meet another party's obligation if that party fails to do so. A personal guarantee makes an individual, rather than a company, liable, and it usually survives the sale of the business unless the lender releases it. Joint and several liability means each guarantor can be pursued for the whole amount, with the lender free to choose whom to pursue, so two guarantors of a $250,000 loan do not each owe $125,000. Exposure at default is the amount outstanding when default occurs, which may equal the facility limit rather than the drawn balance. Probability of default is the likelihood of default within a stated period, usually a year. Recovery is the share of exposure recovered through collateral, sale of assets or payments after default, and loss given default is its complement. Expected loss is exposure multiplied by probability of default multiplied by loss given default, and it is an average across many similar cases rather than a prediction for one case.
depth.mechanism: Guarantees behave differently from loans because their cost is concentrated in a state that is correlated with the guarantor's other risks. A business owner's guarantee is most likely to be called when the business is failing, which is also when the owner's income, other assets and borrowing capacity are weakest. That correlation is why expected loss understates the damage: the average assumes the bad case is drawn independently, while in practice the guarantee, the owner's equity and the owner's income all deteriorate together. The legal mechanics then determine how much is owed. A capped guarantee limits the amount; an unlimited guarantee does not. A guarantee of interest and costs as well as principal increases exposure above the face amount. Joint and several liability lets the lender recover the whole balance from any one guarantor, which makes the practical exposure the full amount even when several people signed. Release provisions matter as much as the cap: many guarantees survive restructuring, and a lender may require a new guarantee as a condition of amending a facility, which resets the clock rather than ending the obligation.
depth.secondExample: Take a larger facility with a lower probability and a weaker recovery. A company guarantees 100 percent of a $600,000 loan made to a supplier it depends on. The probability of default is 2.5 percent and recovery is 20 percent, so loss given default is 80 percent and expected loss is $600,000 multiplied by 0.025 multiplied by 0.80, which is $12,000 a year. If the guarantee is called and the obligation is refinanced at 7 percent interest-only, the annual cost is $42,000. The example shows why the probability is the least important of the three inputs at the decision stage: a 2.5 percent probability is half the 4 percent in the first example, yet the annual cash cost in the bad state is more than twice as large, because the exposure is three times bigger and the recovery is weaker. A guarantor who focuses on the probability will underrate a large, poorly secured exposure and overrate a small, well secured one.
depth.mistake: Multiplying the probability by the face amount and stopping is the commonest error, because it ignores both the guarantee percentage and the recovery. Treating expected loss as a budget line is the second, as though the guarantee cost $5,200 a year, when in fact nothing is paid in most years and $200,000 is payable in a few. Forgetting that joint and several liability makes each guarantor liable for the whole amount is the third, and it matters whenever more than one person signs. The fourth is assuming the guarantee ends when the business is sold, when the contract usually says otherwise. A diagnostic that catches all four: write the exposure as a number, not a percentage, identify the cap and whether interest and costs are included, state who else is liable and on what basis, and compute the annual cash cost of a call alongside the expected loss. If the register shows only an expected loss, it has priced the risk and hidden the obligation.
depth.application: Build a guarantee register with one row per guarantee and eight columns: the borrower, the facility limit, the guaranteed percentage, the resulting exposure, the cap and whether interest and costs are covered, the assumed probability of default, the assumed recovery, and the annual cash cost if called at a stated interest rate. Add two derived columns: expected loss, which is exposure times probability times loss given default, and the coverage impact, which is the annual cash cost divided by the income or cash flow that would have to absorb it. Complete the register when every guarantee has a number in the exposure column, when the cap and the interest and costs question are answered, and when the worst single call is compared with liquid reserves. It fails when the register records only a probability, when joint and several liability is treated as an equal split, or when the guarantee is omitted because it is contingent. Guarantee law, release provisions and lender practice differ by jurisdiction and by contract, so the document governs.
depth.summary: A guarantee is a liability with a probability attached, not a disclosure item. Convert the percentage to an exposure, apply the unrecovered share, and you have an expected loss; apply an interest rate to the exposure and you have the annual cash obligation in the bad state. The expected loss prices the risk, the cash call sizes the damage, and the correlation between the business failing and the guarantor's other finances is why the second number governs decisions.

questions.prompt: A borrower has $196,000 outstanding on a loan at 6.25 percent with 180 monthly payments left, so the payment is $1,680.55. A lender offers 5.50 percent over a fresh 180 months, charging closing costs of $4,200 and a prepayment penalty of 1.5 percent of the balance. Compute the new payment, the monthly saving and the number of months before the upfront cost is recovered.
questions.answer: The penalty is $2,940 and the new balance is $203,140, so the payment is $1,659.82, the saving is $20.73 a month, and the break-even is 344.5 months, which is longer than the 180-month term, so the refinance never recovers its cost
questions.distractor: The rate falls by 0.75 percentage points on $196,000, which is about $1,470 a year, so the $7,140 of upfront cost is recovered in under five years and the refinance is clearly worthwhile
questions.correction: Applying the rate difference to the balance is not a payment calculation. The payment falls only from $1,680.55 to $1,659.82 because the upfront cost is financed into the new balance and the term is unchanged at 180 months. Total interest does fall, from $106,498.79 to $95,628.20, a saving of $10,870.59, but that saving accrues over fifteen years while the $7,140 is paid in month one. Dividing $7,140 by $20.73 gives 344.5 months, so at any exit before that point, including the end of the term, the borrower is behind. The error is treating a rate change as a saving rather than pricing the cost of obtaining it.

questions.prompt: A 5/1 adjustable-rate mortgage of $280,000 started at 5.75 percent over 360 months, giving a payment of $1,634.00. At the first reset the index is 5.20 percent, the margin is 2.50 percent, the initial cap is 2.00 percentage points and the balance is $259,734.12 with 300 months left. Compute the rate that applies and the new payment.
questions.answer: The fully indexed rate is 7.70 percent, which sits below the 7.75 percent initial cap, so 7.70 percent applies and the payment becomes $1,953.33, an increase of $319.33 or 19.54 percent
questions.distractor: The rate resets to the 7.75 percent initial cap because the cap is the rate the lender is entitled to charge, so the payment becomes about $2,020 and the increase is 23.6 percent
questions.correction: The cap is a ceiling, not a target. The margin plus the index gives 7.70 percent, and because 7.70 is below the 7.75 ceiling the borrower pays 7.70. Recomputing the payment means amortising the remaining balance of $259,734.12 over the remaining 300 months at the new rate, not recomputing the original loan over 360 months. That gives $1,953.33 against the $1,634.00 the borrower was paying, an increase of $319.33. The learner who uses the cap as the rate overstates the payment by roughly $67 a month and misreads how a cap works.

questions.prompt: A business can lease a machine for 48 monthly payments of $1,540 with no residual, or borrow $64,000 at 8.00 percent over 48 months and buy it. Total lease payments are $73,920 and total loan payments are $74,996.50. Compute the interest rate implicit in the lease and state which option is cheaper.
questions.answer: The 48 payments of $1,540 discount to $64,000 at 7.25 percent a year, so the lease carries an implicit rate 0.75 points below the 8.00 percent loan and costs $1,076.50 less in total payments
questions.distractor: The lease is cheaper because $73,920 is less than $74,996.50, and the implicit rate is 8.00 percent because that is the rate the bank quoted on the equivalent loan
questions.correction: The lease rate is whatever rate makes the 48 payments equal the $64,000 the machine costs today, and it is 7.25 percent, not the bank's 8.00 percent. Comparing totals alone gives the right ordering here but no rate, so it cannot be used when the terms differ in length or when a residual is involved. The gap of $1,076.50 is the interest saved, and it exists because the lessor is pricing the money 0.75 points cheaper than the bank. Reverse the numbers and the same method shows a lease priced above the loan: if the payment were $1,600, the implicit rate would rise above 8.00 percent and the lease would lose.

questions.prompt: A US exporter expects EUR 900,000 in 120 days. The spot rate is 1.0790 dollars per euro and the 120-day forward is 1.0725. Compute the dollars locked in by the forward, the cost of cover against the spot rate, and the annualised cost. Then state the outcome if the spot rate is 1.0400 at payment.
questions.answer: The forward locks $965,250 against $971,100 at spot, a cost of $5,850 or 0.60 percent over 120 days, which annualises to about 1.83 percent, and if spot falls to 1.0400 the unhedged receipt is $936,000, which is $29,250 below the forward
questions.distractor: The forward costs 0.65 cents per euro, which is 0.65 percent, and since that is the annual cost of cover the exporter pays about 0.65 percent a year for certainty
questions.correction: Two errors sit in that reading. The 0.0065 dollar difference is a cost per euro, not a percentage; as a percentage of the spot rate it is 0.0065 divided by 1.0790, or 0.60 percent, and that is the cost over 120 days rather than over a year. Annualising means multiplying by 365 divided by 120, which gives 1.83 percent. The second error is treating the forward cost as a pure expense: if the spot rate falls to 1.0400 the exporter receives $936,000 unhedged, so the forward is worth $29,250 relative to that outcome. Cover is insurance priced at 1.83 percent a year, and its value depends on the scenario, not on the forward points alone.

questions.prompt: A owner personally guarantees 100 percent of a $400,000 business loan. The lender's own data imply a 3 percent annual probability of default and 25 percent recovery in the event of default. Compute the expected loss on the guarantee and the annual debt service the owner would face if the guarantee were called at 8 percent interest-only.
questions.answer: Expected loss is $400,000 multiplied by 0.03 multiplied by 0.75, which is $9,000 a year, while a call would put $32,000 of annual interest on the owner, or 26.7 percent of $120,000 of personal income
questions.distractor: Expected loss is $12,000, because 3 percent of $400,000 is $12,000 and the guarantee covers the whole balance
questions.correction: Multiplying the probability by the exposure gives the loss only if nothing is recovered. With 25 percent recovery the lender bears 75 percent of the loss, so the guaranteed loss is $400,000 times 0.03 times 0.75, which is $9,000. The expected loss is also the smaller number in the decision: the guarantee is a contingent claim on the owner's cash flow, and a call converts it into $32,000 a year of interest at 8 percent, which is 26.7 percent of $120,000 of income before any principal. The learner who stops at expected loss treats a low-probability event as a small cost, when the obligation in the bad state is the number that constrains other borrowing.

units.title: Long-Dated Money: Escalation, Depreciation, Pensions and Estates

lessons.title: Escalation clauses: caps, floors and the arithmetic of an index-linked contract
lessons.explanation: Lesson 57 treated inflation as a force acting on a plan over a long horizon, and lesson 68 showed how a tax is collected on a transaction and remitted later. This lesson deals with a third use of an index: a clause in a contract that raises the price by a published rate each year. The clause looks like a formality and behaves like a derivative, because it transfers a defined part of the inflation risk from one party to the other. Five terms determine the outcome. The reference index names what is measured, commonly a consumer price index. The base period fixes the starting value and the month from which changes are counted. The review frequency states how often the price changes, usually annually. The floor and cap bound each change, and together they form a collar. The lag states how far in advance of the review the index value must have been published. The arithmetic is compounding: each review applies to the current charge, not to the original price, so a 4 percent cap held for four reviews raises the charge by 16.99 percent, not 16 percent. Lesson 51 showed how compounding at scale bends a curve late and where intuition breaks; here the same mechanism operates inside a legal document, and the seller or buyer who reads only the annual percentage will misjudge the total.
lessons.example: A five-year services contract starts at $480,000 a year with an annual review indexed to consumer prices, subject to a 4 percent cap and no floor. At a steady 3.5 percent, the path is $480,000, $496,800, $514,188, $532,184.58 and $550,811.04, a five-year total of $2,573,983.62. At 5.5 percent the cap binds every year, so the path is $480,000, $499,200, $519,168, $539,934.72 and $561,532.11, a total of $2,599,834.83. Uncapped, the same 5.5 percent would produce $594,635.83 in year five and a total of $2,678,923.69, so the cap is worth $79,088.86 over the term to the buyer. Now compare the capped contract with a fixed 2.5 percent escalator, which gives $529,830.19 in year five and $2,523,037.69 over five years. The capped CPI contract costs $76,797.14 more than the fixed escalator, which is the price the buyer pays for the chance that inflation runs below 2.5 percent and the protection if it runs above 4. The cap has also not frozen the charge: year five is 16.99 percent above year one, which is 1.04 to the fourth power minus one, and that cumulative increase is what belongs in the budget, not the 4 percent annual figure.
lessons.question: A four-year supply contract starts at $150,000 a year with an annual CPI review, a 3 percent cap and no floor. CPI runs at 4.2 percent each year. What are the annual charges and the four-year total, and how much does the cap save against an uncapped clause?
lessons.answer: The cap binds each year, so the charges are $150,000, $154,500, $159,135 and $163,909.05, a total of $627,544.05, which is $11,325.46 less than the $638,869.51 an uncapped clause would produce
lessons.distractor: The charges are $150,000, $156,300, $162,872.25 and $169,712.72, a total of $638,885, because the clause applies the 4.2 percent index each year and the cap only applies once the cumulative increase exceeds 3 percent
lessons.correction: The cap applies to each review, not to the cumulative increase, so every increase is 3 percent and the path compounds at 1.03. The distractor applies the index and produces the uncapped total, which is $638,869.51 rather than the $638,885 quoted, and it misstates the cap's mechanics in a way that would lead a buyer to under-budget by $11,325.46 over four years. The cumulative effect is still material: 1.03 to the third power is 9.27 percent, so the year-four charge is 9.27 percent above year one even though no single increase exceeded 3 percent. Two habits prevent the error: compute the path year by year and sum it, and compare the total with the base multiplied by the number of years, because the difference is the true cost of the clause.

depth.definitions: An escalation clause, also called an indexation or uplift clause, adjusts a contract price by reference to a published index. The reference index is the series named in the contract, such as a national consumer price index, and the contract should name the publisher and the series, because similarly named indices can differ. The base period is the month whose index value is the starting point for the first calculation. The lag is the interval between the reference month and the review date, and it exists because index values are published with a delay. A floor sets a minimum increase, so the price rises even when the index falls, and a cap sets a maximum; together they form a collar. A fixed escalator raises the price by a stated percentage regardless of any index. Compounding means each increase applies to the current charge rather than the original, and the cumulative effect over n reviews is one plus the rate raised to the power n, minus one.
depth.mechanism: The clause transfers risk in a way that is easy to misread because it has two settings. With no floor and a cap, the seller bears the downside and the buyer is protected from the upside, so the seller is paying for the cap in the form of foregone revenue in high-inflation years. With a floor and no cap, the positions reverse. A collar with both limits narrows the range for both parties, and the narrower the collar, the more the contract resembles a fixed price with a small adjustment mechanism. The lag matters because the index used at a review is already historical: in a period of falling inflation, a lagged index overstates the current rate, and in a period of rising inflation it understates it, so the clause systematically lags the economy by one publication cycle. Index substitution is the quiet risk. If the named index is discontinued or redefined, the contract's fallback provision decides what happens, and a fallback to a broader or narrower measure can shift the price materially. Finally, the review mechanism should state whether the increase applies to the whole charge or only to a labour or materials component, because a clause applied to the whole price overcompensates when the indexed cost is a fraction of the total.
depth.secondExample: Take a contract with a floor that binds. A three-year agreement starts at GBP 1,200,000 with an annual CPI review, a 1 percent floor and a 3 percent cap. CPI prints 0.4 percent in both review years. The floor overrides the index, so the charges are GBP 1,200,000, GBP 1,212,000 and GBP 1,224,120, a total of GBP 3,636,120 against GBP 3,600,000 at a flat charge. The floor costs the buyer GBP 36,120 over three years in a period when the measured index was close to zero. That is the correct way to read a floor: it is not a protection against inflation, it is a minimum payment to the seller, and its cost is highest exactly when inflation is lowest. A buyer comparing a floored contract with an unfloored one should price the floor as the expected value of the gap between the floor and the index across the scenarios considered, and should check whether the cap is wide enough to offset it in the years when inflation is high.
depth.mistake: The recurring errors are mechanical. Adding the annual percentages instead of compounding understates a four-year 4 percent path by about 1 percent of the base, which is small, and understates a ten-year path by much more. Applying each year's percentage to the original base rather than the current charge produces a straight line instead of a curve and understates the later years. Ignoring the floor produces a path that is too low in low-inflation years, which is the case the floor was written for. Using the wrong index, or the right index from the wrong month, produces a path that is defensible on its face and wrong in fact. A diagnostic that catches all four: write the first three years of the path by hand, check that each year equals the previous year multiplied by one plus the applied rate, check the applied rate against the index, floor and cap for that review, and confirm the reference month against the published release date. If the hand calculation and the spreadsheet disagree, the clause has been misread rather than mis-keyed.
depth.application: Take a contract with an escalation clause, or construct a realistic one, and build a review table with six columns: review date, reference month and index value, index change since the previous reference, applied rate after floor and cap, annual charge, and cumulative change from year one. Populate three scenarios over the contract term: the index at its most recent published rate, at zero, and at a rate above the cap. Sum the charges in each scenario and compare each total with the base multiplied by the number of years. Complete the table when the cumulative change is stated for every year, when the floor and cap have each been tested in at least one scenario, and when the lag between the reference month and the review date is written down. It fails when the annual rate is added rather than compounded, when the index is applied to the base, or when the total is quoted without the year-by-year path. Index definitions, publication lags and fallback provisions are contractual and jurisdictional, so the document and the named series govern, not the general description here.
depth.summary: An escalation clause is a compounding formula with two limits. Name the index, fix the base period, note the lag, apply floor and cap to each review, and compound from the current charge. Then check the total against the base times the years, because the gap between them is the cost of the clause, and the annual percentage on its own will always understate it.

readings.title: Office for National Statistics, Consumer price inflation, UK: latest bulletin
readings.note: Read the latest movements section, which for the September 2026 release states that the Consumer Prices Index rose by 3.5 percent in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1 percent the previous month, that CPIH rose by 3.6 percent, and that CPI rose by 0.4 percent on the month. Read it for the three quantities this lesson distinguishes: the annual rate, the monthly rate and the difference between two similar indices. A contract that names CPI and a party that tracks CPIH are measuring different things, and the bulletin shows how far apart they can be in a single month. The release is revised and superseded monthly, so the figures quoted here describe one publication and not a permanent state.

readings.title: Bank of England, Inflation and the 2% target
readings.note: Read the statement that the Government sets a target of keeping inflation at 2 percent, that CPI is the measure targeted, and that if CPI misses the target by more than one percentage point on either side the Governor must write to the Government explaining why, which the page describes as CPI above 3 percent or below 1 percent. Read it for the institutional reason an index is a usable contract reference: it is measured by an independent statistical agency against a published basket, and the central bank's remit makes the measure a matter of public record. The target is a policy objective, not a forecast, and the page does not predict the rate a contract will experience.

readings.title: Federal Reserve Board, H.15 Selected Interest Rates
readings.note: Read the description of the Treasury inflation-indexed series, which the release lists at constant maturities of 5, 7, 10, 20 and 30 years and which are derived from TIPS rather than from nominal Treasuries. Read it alongside the nominal constant maturity description, because the difference between the two yields is the market's price of expected inflation over that horizon, which is the number a party to an indexed contract would compare with the cap and floor on offer. The series is a market yield, not a forecast of the consumer price index, and the two can diverge for long periods.
