lessons.title: Depreciation and disposal: the after-tax cost of an asset you will later sell
lessons.explanation: Lesson 73 compared leasing with buying and used a depreciation schedule as an input. This lesson takes that schedule apart, because the timing of the deductions is often the largest controllable number in the purchase decision. Depreciation is not a cash outflow. It is an allocation of the asset's cost across tax years, and its only cash effect is the tax that is not paid because the deduction reduces taxable income. That effect is the tax shield, equal to the deduction multiplied by the marginal tax rate, and its value depends on when the deductions arrive and on the rate used to discount them. Two rules shape the timing. The recovery period assigns the asset to a class, commonly five or seven years for equipment, and the method front-loads the deductions within that period. The convention decides how much of a year is allowed in the first year and the last: the half-year convention gives half a year in each, which spreads six years of deductions across seven tax years, while the mid-quarter convention applies when a large share of assets is placed in service late in the year. Disposal then settles the account, because the difference between the sale price and the adjusted basis is taxed, and for most equipment that gain is ordinary income rather than a capital gain.
lessons.example: A business buys equipment for $180,000 and places it in service in the current year. It is five-year property, the half-year convention applies and the marginal tax rate is 24 percent. The deductions are $36,000, $57,600, $34,560, $20,736, $20,736 and $10,368, which total $180,000 across six tax years. The shields are $8,640, $13,824, $8,294.40, $4,976.64, $4,976.64 and $2,488.32, totalling $43,200. At an 8 percent discount rate the present value is $35,049.27, so the effective after-tax cost is $180,000 minus $35,049.27, which is $144,950.73, or 80.53 percent of the purchase price. Suppose the business instead elects to expense the full cost under section 179, which is available for this asset because the annual limit is $2,500,000 and the phase-out begins above $4,000,000 of qualifying property placed in service in 2025. The shield is then $43,200 received immediately, worth $43,200 in present value, which is $8,150.73 more than the depreciated path. Now suppose the asset is sold for $90,000 after three years. The adjusted basis is $180,000 minus the first three deductions, which is $51,840, so the gain is $38,160 and, because the asset is section 1245 property, that gain is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken, taxed at 24 percent, which is $9,158.40. The after-tax proceeds are $80,841.60.
lessons.question: A firm buys equipment for $96,000, depreciates it as five-year property with the half-year convention, and pays tax at 22 percent. The six deductions are $19,200, $30,720, $18,432, $11,059.20, $11,059.20 and $5,529.60. What is the present value of the tax shield at 8 percent, and what tax is due if the asset is sold for $45,000 after three years?
lessons.answer: The shields total $21,120 and are worth $17,135.20 at 8 percent, so the effective cost is $78,864.80, and a sale for $45,000 after three years gives a $17,352 gain on a $27,648 basis, taxed as ordinary recapture at 22 percent for $3,817.44
lessons.distractor: The shield is worth $21,120 because 22 percent of $96,000 is $21,120 and the timing of the deductions does not change the total, and the sale produces a capital gain of $45,000 minus the remaining book value, taxed at the capital rate
lessons.correction: The $21,120 is the undiscounted total, and the deductions arrive across six tax years, so at 8 percent the present value is $17,135.20, which is 19 percent less than the total. Timing matters more as the discount rate rises and as the recovery period lengthens, which is why the same asset can be worth several thousand dollars more to a business that can expense it immediately. On the sale, the adjusted basis is $96,000 minus $19,200, $30,720 and $18,432, which is $27,648, so the gain is $17,352. Section 1245 treats that gain as ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken, so the tax is $3,817.44 at 22 percent, not a capital rate. Treating recapture as a capital gain understates the tax and overstates the net proceeds by the difference between the two rates.

depth.definitions: Basis is the amount invested in an asset for tax purposes, usually cost including installation and freight. The recovery period is the number of years over which the basis is recovered under the applicable table, determined by the asset class. MACRS is the modified accelerated cost recovery system, which applies declining-balance percentages to the basis and switches to straight line where that produces a larger deduction. The half-year convention treats an asset placed in service at any point in the year as placed in service at mid-year, which gives half a year of deduction in the first year and half in the year after the recovery period ends. The mid-quarter convention applies instead when more than 40 percent of the year's depreciable basis is placed in service in the final quarter. Section 179 is an election to deduct the cost of qualifying property in the year it is placed in service, subject to an annual limit and a phase-out. The adjusted basis is cost minus accumulated deductions. Recapture is the treatment of gain on sale as ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken on section 1245 property, which includes most equipment.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that makes depreciation worth analysing is the combination of a fixed total and a variable timing. The total deductions equal the basis whatever method is used, assuming the asset is held and then scrapped, so the only thing a method can change is when the shield arrives, and the value of arriving earlier is the discount rate. An accelerated method therefore dominates a straight-line method for a taxpayer with taxable income, while a taxpayer with no taxable income may prefer to slow the deductions so they are not wasted against a zero rate. The half-year convention adds a seventh tax year to a five-year asset, which lowers the present value slightly compared with a schedule that fits inside five years, and the mid-quarter convention can lower it further by allowing only a quarter of a year in the first year. Disposal interacts with all of this. Selling before the schedule is exhausted leaves an adjusted basis, and the tax on the difference is computed by character: ordinary recapture first, then capital gain for any excess over original cost. A sale below the adjusted basis produces a loss, and whether that loss is deductible depends on the character of the asset and the taxpayer's situation.
depth.secondExample: Take a smaller asset with the same structure and a lower tax rate. A firm buys equipment for $95,000, five-year property, half-year convention, tax at 24 percent. The deductions are $19,000, $30,400, $18,240, $10,944, $10,944 and $5,472, and the shields are $4,560, $7,296, $4,377.60, $2,626.56, $2,626.56 and $1,313.28, totalling $22,800. The present value at 8 percent is $18,498.23, so the effective cost is $76,501.77, or 80.53 percent of the price, which is the same percentage as the larger example because both use the same table and the same rate. That identity is useful: for five-year property with the half-year convention and an 8 percent discount rate, the shield is worth 19.47 percent of cost at a 24 percent tax rate, and that ratio can be applied to any purchase price without rebuilding the schedule. Change any input and the ratio changes: at a 12 percent discount rate the same shield is worth less, and at a 32 percent tax rate the effective cost falls to about 74 percent of price.
depth.mistake: Deducting the full cost in year one is the mistake that distorts everything after it, overstating the first-year shield by a factor of five. Using accounting depreciation, which is often straight line and sometimes based on a different life, is the second, because it substitutes a book convention for the tax table. Forgetting recapture on disposal and treating the whole gain as a capital gain is the third, and it understates the tax on a sale. Discounting at the pre-tax borrowing rate is the fourth, which understates the present value of every future deduction and makes immediate expensing look less valuable than it is. A diagnostic that catches all four: write the six deductions, check that they sum to the basis, discount them at the after-tax rate, and then compute the disposal tax separately using the adjusted basis at the sale date. If the six deductions do not sum to the basis, the table or the convention has been misapplied.
depth.application: Take an asset you could plausibly buy and build a two-page calculation. Page one: the cost including installation, the recovery period and convention, the six annual deductions from the applicable table, the tax rate you assume, the annual shield, and the present value of the shield at your after-tax discount rate. Page two: the disposal case, with a sale in year three at three prices, high, near the adjusted basis, and low, and for each the adjusted basis, the gain or loss, its character, the tax, and the after-tax proceeds. Complete the calculation when the deductions sum to the basis, when the present value uses the same discount rate as the purchase decision, and when at least one disposal case produces ordinary recapture. It fails when depreciation is treated as a cash cost, when the full cost is expensed without checking an election, or when the sale is assumed to be tax-free. Recovery periods, conventions, election limits and recapture rules are specific to US federal income tax and change with legislation, so the current form instructions govern.
depth.summary: Depreciation converts part of an asset's cost into a stream of tax deductions, and the stream is worth less than its total because it arrives over years. Discount the shields at the after-tax rate to get the effective cost, compare that with immediate expensing where an election is available, and settle the disposal separately, because recapture is ordinary income and the adjusted basis at the sale date, not the original cost, determines the tax.

readings.title: Internal Revenue Service, Publication 946, How to Depreciate Property
readings.note: Read the section on which recovery period applies, the table showing five-year and seven-year property, and the discussion of the half-year and mid-quarter conventions, including the 40 percent test for the mid-quarter convention. Read also the section 179 limits: for tax years beginning in 2025 the maximum deduction is $2,500,000, reduced by the amount by which the cost of section 179 property placed in service exceeds $4,000,000, and for 2026 the figures are $2,560,000 and $4,090,000. Those limits are indexed and change annually, so check the year you are modelling. The publication gives the table percentages used in this lesson and is US federal tax guidance.

readings.title: Internal Revenue Service, Publication 544, Sales and Other Dispositions of Assets
readings.note: Read the section headed gain treated as ordinary income and the definition of section 1245 property, which covers depreciable personal property and explains why gain on equipment is recaptured as ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken. Read it before computing any after-tax sale proceeds, because the character of the gain, not just its size, determines the tax. The publication also distinguishes a sale at a gain from a sale at a loss and sets out when each is recognised, which is the part of the disposal calculation most often skipped.

readings.title: Internal Revenue Service, Publication 551, Basis of Assets
readings.note: Read the sections on cost basis and on adjustments to basis, including the deduction for depreciation, which is how the adjusted basis at a sale date is derived. Read also the inherited property section, which states that the basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally the fair market value at the date of death, with an alternative valuation date available in some cases; that rule is the link to the inheritance lesson later in this level. The publication is US federal tax guidance and the basis rules differ for gifts, trusts and business entities.

lessons.title: A promised income for life: valuing a pension and reading a transfer value
lessons.explanation: Lesson 48 evaluated an annuity as a product and lesson 46 examined what a bad sequence of returns does to a retirement plan. This lesson values a promise rather than a product: a defined benefit pension that pays a stated income from a stated age, usually for life and usually rising each year with an index. The promise has no market price to look up, so its value has to be constructed from four inputs. The annual benefit fixes the starting payment. The indexation rule fixes how it grows. The expected duration fixes how many payments there may be, and it is an expectation over a population rather than a prediction for one person. The discount rate converts the future payments into a present value, and it is the assumption that moves the answer most. A transfer value, sometimes called a cash equivalent transfer value, is the price a scheme offers to exchange the promise for a lump sum now. Comparing the two is not a matter of adding up the payments; it is a matter of finding the discount rate implied by the offer and asking whether that rate is a fair price for the risk being given up.
lessons.example: A scheme promises GBP 24,000 a year from age 67, rising by 3 percent each year, for an assumed 22 years, with the first payment one year after retirement. At a 4.5 percent discount rate the present value is GBP 435,926.14. The calculation discounts each payment by its own year: 24,000 divided by 1.045, plus 24,720 divided by 1.045 squared, and so on to year 22, which is 24,000 times 1.03 to the 21st power, or 44,647.07, divided by 1.045 to the 22nd. Summing the series gives the figure above. Change only the discount rate to 6 percent and the value falls to GBP 374,617.23, a reduction of 14.1 percent for a 1.5 point change. Remove the indexation and the value at 4.5 percent falls to GBP 330,826.19, so the annual 3 percent uplift is worth GBP 105,099.95, or 31.8 percent of the level value. Now suppose the scheme offers a transfer value of GBP 310,000. Solving for the rate that equates the indexed payments to that lump sum gives 8.03 percent, which is far above the 4.5 percent assumption. On these inputs the offer is priced at a discount of 28.9 percent to the 4.5 percent valuation, and the arithmetic alone cannot say whether that is generous or cheap; it says what the offer assumes.
lessons.question: A pension promises GBP 15,000 a year for 18 years, rising 2 percent a year, first payment in one year. At a 4.5 percent discount rate the value is GBP 211,973.74 and at a level (no indexation) it is GBP 182,399.88. A transfer value of GBP 210,000 is offered. What does the arithmetic say?
lessons.answer: The indexed promise is worth GBP 211,973.74, the transfer value of GBP 210,000 is within 1 percent of that figure, and the offer implies a discount rate of about 4.61 percent, so the quote is close to the valuation rather than obviously good or bad
lessons.distractor: The promise is worth GBP 270,000 because 15,000 a year for 18 years is 270,000, so the GBP 210,000 transfer value is a loss of GBP 60,000 and should be refused
lessons.correction: The GBP 270,000 is an undiscounted sum, and money received in year 18 is not worth the same as money received today. At 4.5 percent the indexed stream is worth 211,973.74, and the transfer value of 210,000 is 1 percent below that, not 22 percent below it. The implied rate of 4.61 percent is the useful comparison: it says the scheme is pricing the promise at slightly more than the 4.5 percent used in the valuation, which is a small difference rather than a large one. Whether to transfer also depends on things the arithmetic cannot see, including the security of the scheme, the value of survivor benefits, the tax treatment of a lump sum, and the cost of buying an equivalent income in the market. The error to avoid is treating the undiscounted total as the benchmark, because it makes every transfer value look like a loss.

depth.definitions: A defined benefit pension promises an income calculated by a formula, typically an accrual rate applied to years of service and to salary, rather than a pot of contributions. The accrual rate is the fraction of salary earned per year of service, for example one sixtieth. Indexation is the annual increase applied to the benefit in payment, and it may be a fixed rate, a consumer price index, or a cap and floor around an index. A transfer value is the lump sum a scheme offers in exchange for the promise, calculated on actuarial assumptions about longevity, investment returns and inflation. An annuity is an income purchased with a lump sum, and the two are comparable only if the annuity has the same indexation, survivor benefits and guarantees. The discount rate is the return used to convert future payments into present value, and it should reflect the risk of the promise rather than the return the member hopes to earn. Longevity is the distribution of possible lifetimes, not a single number, and using a single life expectancy understates the value of a lifetime promise because the payments continue for survivors.
depth.mechanism: The present value of an indexed lifetime income is a growing annuity, and the growing annuity is unusually sensitive to the gap between the discount rate and the indexation rate. When the two are close, the denominator of the formula becomes small and the value becomes large, which is why a 1.5 point change in the discount rate moved the first example by 14.1 percent. The second mechanism is the transfer value itself. A scheme prices it on its own funding assumptions, which reflect the assets it holds and the regulator's requirements, and those assumptions need not match the member's opportunity cost. That is why the implied rate is the right diagnostic: it extracts the scheme's price and lets the member compare it with what they could earn elsewhere and with what an equivalent annuity would cost. The third mechanism is risk transfer. A promise carries the scheme's covenant, the protection of any insurance guarantee, and the indexation rule. A lump sum carries investment risk and longevity risk, which the member now bears. Neither is safer in the abstract; they transfer different risks, and the arithmetic values the income stream, not the risk.
depth.secondExample: Take a US-style promise quoted in dollars per month. A plan pays $2,400 a month, or $28,800 a year, for 20 years with no indexation. At a 5 percent discount rate the value is $358,911.66. At 7 percent it falls to $305,107.61, a reduction of 15 percent for a two point change in the rate, which is the same sensitivity the first example showed in a different form. The undiscounted total is $576,000, and the gap between that and $358,911.66 is 37.7 percent, which is why the undiscounted figure is never the benchmark. Now add indexation at 2 percent and the value at 5 percent rises to a figure above $400,000, because every payment after the first is larger. The lesson generalises: the value of a promise is a function of the benefit, the indexation, the duration and the discount rate, and of those four the discount rate is the one the member controls least and the one that changes the answer most.
depth.mistake: Summing the payments and treating the total as the value is the error that makes every offer look poor, because it ignores discounting. Using a single life expectancy and stopping is the second, which ignores the possibility of living longer and the value of survivor benefits. Valuing an indexed promise as though it were level is the third, and it understates its value by about 24 percent in the first example. The fourth is comparing a transfer value with the scheme's funding position rather than with the promise: a scheme can be well funded and still offer a transfer value that is poor relative to the benefit it is buying out. A diagnostic: compute the present value at three discount rates, compute the implied rate of the offer, and write down what the offer does not include, such as indexation, survivor cover and any early retirement reduction. If the implied rate falls outside the range of rates you would accept for a promise of that risk, the offer is worth questioning.
depth.application: Value a promise using four steps. Step one: write the annual benefit, the indexation rule, the starting age and the assumed duration, and note that the duration is an expectation rather than a certainty. Step two: compute the present value at three discount rates, one below, one at, and one above your opportunity cost, and record the range rather than a single number. Step three: if a transfer value is on offer, solve for the rate that equates the payments to the offer, and compare that implied rate with your range. Step four: list what the calculation leaves out, including survivor benefits, early retirement reductions, tax on the lump sum versus tax on the income, the security of the scheme and any insurance guarantee. Complete the exercise when the implied rate is stated and the omissions are named. It fails when the payments are summed without discounting, when indexation is ignored, or when a single life expectancy is presented as the duration. Pension rules, transfer advice requirements and tax treatment differ by jurisdiction; in the UK many transfers require regulated advice, and the rules change, so the current requirements must be checked.
depth.summary: A pension promise is a growing annuity, and its value is the discounted sum of the payments, not the sum. The discount rate, the indexation and the duration set the answer, and the offer's implied rate is the number to compare. A transfer value is a price for a risk transfer, so the arithmetic can say what the offer assumes but not whether the risk being given up was worth keeping.

lessons.title: Inheritance arithmetic: thresholds, taper and the marginal rate that surprises
lessons.explanation: Lesson 49 covered the documents that decide who receives an estate, and lesson 77 covered the basis that sets the tax on a later sale. This lesson connects the two by pricing what the recipients actually inherit. Inheritance tax is levied on the value of an estate above a threshold, and the threshold is not a single number: it is a basic allowance, an additional allowance for a residence left to direct descendants, and a taper that withdraws the additional allowance as the estate grows. The interaction produces effective rates that differ from the headline rate in both directions. Below the taper the effective rate on the whole estate rises with size because the fixed allowance is a smaller share of a larger estate. Inside the taper the marginal rate exceeds the headline rate, because each additional pound both attracts tax and reduces an allowance. Above the taper the marginal rate returns to the headline rate. A calculation that applies the headline rate to the excess over a simple threshold will therefore be wrong in the middle of the range, which is where most estates of this size sit. Jurisdiction matters throughout, and the UK and US rules share a structure but not the numbers.
lessons.example: A UK estate is worth GBP 1,850,000, including a home of GBP 650,000 left to the deceased's children. The nil-rate band is GBP 325,000 and the residence nil-rate band is GBP 175,000, so the total allowance is GBP 500,000 and the taxable estate is GBP 1,350,000. At 40 percent the tax is GBP 540,000, which is 29.19 percent of the estate. Now raise the estate to GBP 2,300,000 and keep everything else the same. The residence band tapers by GBP 1 for every GBP 2 above GBP 2,000,000, so the excess of GBP 300,000 reduces it by GBP 150,000, leaving GBP 25,000. The allowance is GBP 350,000, the taxable estate is GBP 1,950,000, and the tax is GBP 780,000, or 33.91 percent of the estate. Inside that taper zone the marginal rate is 60 percent: an extra GBP 1,000 of estate adds GBP 500 to the taxable amount through the lost band and GBP 400 of tax on the GBP 1,000 itself. At GBP 3,000,000 the residence band is gone entirely, the allowance is GBP 325,000, and the tax is GBP 1,070,000. The sequence shows why the effective rate is a poor guide to a decision at the margin: the difference between GBP 2,000,000 and GBP 2,350,000 costs 60 pence of tax for every additional pound, which is a steeper rate than any income tax band in the UK.
lessons.question: An estate is worth GBP 1,720,000, including a home left to the children. With a nil-rate band of GBP 325,000 and a residence nil-rate band of GBP 175,000, tapered above GBP 2,000,000, what is the tax and the effective rate?
lessons.answer: The estate is below the taper threshold, so the full GBP 500,000 allowance applies, the taxable estate is GBP 1,220,000, the tax is GBP 488,000, and the effective rate is 28.37 percent
lessons.distractor: The allowance is GBP 325,000 because the residence band only applies to estates below GBP 500,000, so the taxable estate is GBP 1,395,000 and the tax is GBP 558,000
lessons.correction: The residence nil-rate band has no upper value limit of the kind the distractor invents; it applies where a qualifying residence passes to direct descendants and is tapered only above GBP 2,000,000. At GBP 1,720,000 there is no taper, so the allowance is the full GBP 500,000 and the tax is GBP 488,000. The error is worth GBP 70,000, which is 12.5 percent of the correct tax. A second error lurks in the same calculation: the effective rate of 28.37 percent is not the rate that applies to the next pound. Below the taper the marginal rate is the headline 40 percent, because an additional pound neither adds to nor subtracts from the allowance. Confusing the average with the marginal rate is the most common way to misjudge a decision such as whether to make a lifetime gift.

depth.definitions: An estate for inheritance tax purposes is the value of all assets owned at death, less liabilities, plus certain gifts made within a stated period before death. The nil-rate band is the basic threshold below which no tax is charged. The residence nil-rate band is an additional threshold available when a qualifying residence is left to direct descendants, and it is subject to a taper above a stated estate value. The taper reduces the additional band by a fixed amount for every unit by which the estate exceeds the taper threshold, which is why the marginal rate inside that zone exceeds the headline rate. The chargeable estate is the value remaining after allowances, reliefs and exemptions. The headline rate is the statutory rate applied to the chargeable estate. The effective rate is tax divided by the whole estate, and the marginal rate is the tax on the next unit of value; the two coincide only in the range where allowances are fixed. A lifetime gift is a transfer made during life, and gifts within a stated period before death may be brought into the calculation. The step-up in basis, in the US, resets the income tax basis of inherited assets to their value at death.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that produces the surprising marginal rate is the interaction of a fixed threshold with a tapering allowance. A fixed threshold alone produces a marginal rate equal to the headline rate at every point above it, because the threshold does not move. A tapering allowance moves in the opposite direction to the estate, so each additional pound reduces the allowance as well as adding to the chargeable amount, and the two effects add. In the UK case the band falls by 50 pence for every pound of excess, so the chargeable estate rises by GBP 1.50 for each additional GBP 1.00, and at 40 percent the tax rises by 60 pence. The same structure appears in other jurisdictions with different numbers and different reliefs. The second mechanism is the relationship between inheritance tax and capital gains tax. In the US, assets included in an estate generally take a basis equal to their value at death, which removes the pre-death gain from income tax; in the UK there is no equivalent general reset, so an asset may bear inheritance tax at death and capital gains tax on a later sale. Whether a lifetime gift is better than a bequest therefore depends on both taxes, not one.
depth.secondExample: Take the taper zone directly. At GBP 2,100,000 the excess over the GBP 2,000,000 threshold is GBP 100,000, so the residence band is reduced by GBP 50,000 to GBP 125,000, the allowance is GBP 450,000, and the tax is 40 percent of GBP 1,650,000, which is GBP 660,000. At GBP 2,101,000 the band is reduced to GBP 124,500, the allowance is GBP 449,500, and the tax is 40 percent of GBP 1,651,500, which is GBP 660,600. The extra GBP 1,000 of estate has produced GBP 600 of tax, a marginal rate of 60 percent, while the effective rate moved only from 31.43 to 31.44 percent. The gap between those two figures is the whole lesson: at this size an estate is being taxed at 60 pence in the pound on each additional pound, and the average rate barely moves, so a decision about whether to spend, give or insure must be made on the marginal number. The taper ends at GBP 2,350,000, where the residence band reaches zero, and beyond that point the marginal rate returns to 40 percent.
depth.mistake: Applying the headline rate to the excess over a single threshold is the standard error, and it ignores the additional residence band and then, past the taper, its withdrawal. Confusing the effective rate with the marginal rate is the second, and it understates the cost of an extra pound in the taper zone by 20 points. Treating a spouse exemption as unlimited in every circumstance is the third; transfers between spouses are generally exempt, but the exemption interacts with the order of deaths, with the residence band and with the treatment of gifts. The fourth is forgetting that gifts made within the stated period before death are brought back into the calculation, so an estate that looks comfortably below the threshold can be pushed above it by a gift that was intended to reduce it. A diagnostic: compute the tax at the actual value and at the actual value plus GBP 1,000, and divide the difference by 1,000. That gives the marginal rate, and it is the number that should drive any decision about giving, spending or insuring.
depth.application: Compute inheritance tax on a specified estate in four steps. Step one: list the assets and liabilities and state the jurisdiction and the tax year, because both change the numbers. Step two: identify which allowances apply, including the additional residence allowance, and whether the residence passes to a qualifying descendant. Step three: test the taper by comparing the estate with the taper threshold, and reduce the residence allowance by the stated fraction of the excess. Step four: compute tax on the chargeable estate, then compute it again at GBP 1,000 more to obtain the marginal rate. Complete the calculation when the allowance, the chargeable estate, the tax, the effective rate and the marginal rate are all stated separately. It fails when a single threshold is used, when the effective rate is presented as the rate on the next pound, or when gifts within the relevant period are omitted. Inheritance tax rules, reliefs and rates differ by jurisdiction and change with legislation; the UK figures here are the nil-rate band of GBP 325,000 and the residence band of GBP 175,000 with a taper above GBP 2,000,000, and the US figures are the federal exclusion amounts published by the Internal Revenue Service.
depth.summary: Inheritance tax is a threshold calculation with a taper, and the taper is where the arithmetic stops being intuitive. Compute the allowance, reduce the residence band for any excess over the taper threshold, tax the remainder at the headline rate, and then compute the tax on the next GBP 1,000 to find the marginal rate. The effective rate describes the estate; the marginal rate describes the decision.

lessons.title: Capstone: a commitment register that prices everything you have signed
lessons.explanation: Every lesson in this level has priced one kind of obligation: an exit from a loan in lesson 71, a reset in lesson 72, a lease in lesson 73, a currency exposure in lesson 74, a guarantee in lesson 75, an indexed contract in lesson 76, an asset's tax life in lesson 77, a pension promise in lesson 78 and an inheritance threshold in lesson 79. This lesson assembles them into one artefact, a commitment register, because the risk that damages a household or a firm is rarely a single obligation. It is the combination: a mortgage that resets, a lease that runs, a contract that escalates, a guarantee that is called, and a currency that moves, all at once, against a cash flow that was planned when none of them had moved. A register has one row per commitment and eight columns: the annual charge in year one, the charge in the final year, the rate basis, the index or currency, the contingency, the exit cost, the review date, and the measure that applies. Three measures are needed, not one. The run-rate shows the annual burden. The present value shows the size of the commitment relative to the others. The worst case shows what happens if the contingency occurs and the index moves at the same time.
lessons.example: A firm has EBITDA of $840,000 and four committed annual charges. A mortgage costs $28,800, an equipment lease $29,460, an indexed services contract starts at $540,000 with a 3 percent annual cap, and pension contributions are $48,000. Year-one charges total $646,260, so coverage is 1.30 times. By year five the contract has been reviewed four times at the cap, so it reaches $540,000 times 1.03 to the fourth power, which is $607,774.76, and total charges rise to $714,034.76. Coverage falls to 1.176 times, a reduction of 9.5 percent, with no change in EBITDA and no new borrowing. Now add the contingency: a personal guarantee of $240,000 that is called and refinanced at 7 percent interest-only adds $16,800 a year, taking charges to $730,834.76 and coverage to 1.149 times. The register changes the conversation. On a year-one view the firm has 30 percent of headroom; on a year-five view with one contingency realised it has 15 percent, and the difference is entirely visible in the schedule rather than in a forecast. Note also what the register reveals about ranking: the contract is 83.6 percent of year-one charges, so a two point change in its cap matters more than a 20 percent change in the mortgage.
lessons.question: A firm has EBITDA of $1,000,000 and four commitments: a mortgage of $36,000 a year, a lease of $33,600, an indexed contract of $720,000 with a 4 percent cap, and pension contributions of $54,000. A guarantee of $200,000 could be called and refinanced at 8 percent. Compute coverage in year one, year five and in the stressed case.
lessons.answer: Year-one charges are $843,600 and coverage is 1.185, year-five charges are $965,982.80 and coverage is 1.035, and adding $16,000 of interest on a called guarantee gives $981,982.80 and coverage of 1.018, so the firm has almost no headroom in the stressed case
lessons.distractor: Year-one coverage is 1.185 and the 4 percent cap protects the firm, so coverage stays near 1.18 and the guarantee is immaterial because it is contingent and has not been called
lessons.correction: The cap limits each annual increase, not the cumulative one, so four reviews at 4 percent raise the contract by 16.99 percent to $842,382.80 and year-five charges to $965,982.80. Coverage falls from 1.185 to 1.035, which is the difference between comfortable and covenant-tight, even though EBITDA has not changed. The guarantee then does two things: it is not immaterial, because a call adds $16,000 a year and takes coverage to 1.018, and it is correlated with the same conditions that would make the contract harder to renegotiate. The register's value is that all three numbers sit on one page, so the question changes from whether the firm can afford today's commitments to which single commitment would have to be renegotiated first if the stressed case arrived.

depth.definitions: A commitment is a contractual obligation to pay, whether or not it appears as debt on a balance sheet. The run-rate is the annual charge in a stated year, usually the current one. The present value of commitments is the discounted sum of the scheduled charges, and it is the measure that ranks obligations of different durations. Coverage is the ratio of a cash flow measure, such as EBITDA, to committed charges, and a coverage covenant is a contractual minimum. A contingency is an obligation that arises only on an event, such as a guarantee call. The exit cost is the amount payable to end a commitment early, including prepayment penalties, termination fees and residual guarantees. A review date is the date on which the register is re-measured against records. Headroom is the difference between the current ratio and the covenant minimum, in ratio terms or in currency. A sensitivity is a single stated change applied to one input to see how much the answer moves.
depth.mechanism: The register works because it puts three measures against each other and forces the differences to be explained. The run-rate answers what must be paid this year and is the measure a bank account feels. The present value answers how large the commitment is relative to the others and is the measure that prevents a five-year contract from being treated as a one-year expense. The worst case answers whether the firm survives an event and is the measure that prices guarantees and resets. Duration is the link between them: a commitment with a long remaining term has a present value much larger than its annual charge, and the gap grows as the discount rate falls. Correlation is the second mechanism. Commitments rarely move independently: an inflation print that raises the indexed contract also raises the index that resets the mortgage, and the same recession that makes a guarantee call likely reduces EBITDA. A register that tests each commitment separately understates the combined effect, which is why the stressed case should apply at least two adverse changes at once. The third mechanism is exit. A commitment with a 3 percent prepayment penalty and a 45,000 exit fee is not a source of flexibility, and a register that lists only the charges overstates how quickly the firm can respond.
depth.secondExample: Add a currency exposure and an indexed contract to a smaller firm. The firm invoices EUR 300,000 a year at 1.0820, so the dollar equivalent is $324,600, and it covers the exposure at an annualised cost of 2 percent, which is $6,492. Its services contract is $420,000 with a 4 percent cap, and its loan and lease charges are $24,000 and $18,000. Year-one charges including the hedge cost are $468,492 and coverage on EBITDA of $540,000 is 1.153. In year five the contract reaches $420,000 times 1.04 to the fourth power, which is $491,238.70, and charges rise to $539,730.70, so coverage falls to 1.001. The firm is now at its limit with no contingency realised and no currency move beyond the hedge. The register has done its job: it has shown that the indexed contract alone consumes the whole margin over four years, and that the currency hedge, which looked like a cost, is 1.4 percent of the total and irrelevant compared with the escalation clause. Ranking the commitments by size is what makes the next decision obvious.
depth.mistake: Registering only debt is the error that starts the problem, because it omits leases, indexed contracts, guarantees and pension contributions and produces a coverage ratio that is too high. Using year-one charges for a multi-year commitment is the second, and it hides escalation. Measuring each commitment separately and never testing two adverse changes together is the third, which is how a firm discovers too late that the index and the rate moved in the same direction. Omitting exit costs is the fourth, and it overstates flexibility exactly when flexibility is needed. A diagnostic that catches all four: count the rows and check that every signed document with a payment obligation has one, compare the year-one and final-year charge for each row, confirm that the stressed case applies at least two changes at once, and check that every row with a termination right has a number in the exit column. If any of those four checks fails, the register is a list rather than a measurement.
depth.application: Build a commitment register for a household or a firm using eight columns: commitment name, year-one charge, final-year charge, rate basis, index or currency, contingency and its probability, exit cost, and review date. Then add three summary lines. Line one: total year-one charges and the coverage ratio against a stated cash flow measure. Line two: total final-year charges with the same ratio. Line three: the stressed case, applying the contract at its cap, the rate at its reset, and any guarantee called, all at once. Rank the rows by present value at a stated discount rate and write one sentence naming the commitment that dominates. Complete the register when every obligation has a number in every column, when the stressed case is worse than the year-five case, and when the dominant commitment is named with the reason. It fails when a contingent obligation is left blank, when escalation is described in words rather than computed, or when the coverage ratio is quoted for year one only. This is a measurement exercise and not financial advice; covenant definitions and tax treatment are contractual and jurisdictional.
depth.summary: A commitment register converts a pile of signed documents into three numbers: the charge this year, the charge in the final year, and the charge in the stressed case, each against the same cash flow. Rank the rows by present value, put a number in every contingency and exit column, and re-measure on a stated date. The register is the difference between knowing what you owe and knowing what you have promised.

questions.prompt: A three-year services contract starts at GBP 240,000 a year with an indexation clause of CPI with a 1 percent floor and a 3 percent cap. CPI prints 0.2 percent, 0.4 percent and 1.1 percent in the three review years. Compute the annual charges and the total contract value.
questions.answer: The floor binds in the first two reviews, so the charges are GBP 240,000, 242,400, 244,824 and 247,517.06, a total of GBP 974,741.06, which is GBP 254,741.06 above three years at the base rate
questions.distractor: The charges are GBP 240,000, 240,480, 241,442 and 244,098, a total of GBP 966,020, because each year applies the printed CPI to the base amount
questions.correction: Two mechanics are being missed. The floor of 1 percent means a CPI print of 0.2 or 0.4 percent still produces a 1 percent increase, so the first two reviews add GBP 2,400 and GBP 2,424 rather than a few hundred pounds. And each review applies the uplift to the previous year's charge, not to the original base, which is why the third year is 240,000 times 1.01 times 1.01 times 1.011, equal to 247,517.06. The distractor compounds nothing and ignores the floor, understating the three-year total by GBP 8,721.06. A floor is a pricing term with a cost, and it is paid for by the buyer in exactly the years when the index is quiet.

questions.prompt: A business buys equipment for $150,000, depreciates it as five-year property under MACRS with the half-year convention, and pays tax at 25 percent. The first-year deduction is $30,000 and the six annual deductions total $150,000. Compute the present value of the tax shield at 7 percent and the effective after-tax cost. Then compute the tax on a sale for $100,000 after two years.
questions.answer: The shield is worth $31,183.06 in present value, so the effective cost is $118,816.94, and a sale for $100,000 after two years produces a $28,000 gain on a $72,000 basis, taxed at 25 percent as ordinary recapture, which is $7,000
questions.distractor: The shield is worth $37,500 because $150,000 of deductions at 25 percent is $37,500, and the sale produces a $28,000 capital gain taxed at the lower capital rate
questions.correction: The $37,500 is the undiscounted total, and the deductions arrive over six years, so at 7 percent the present value is $31,183.06 and the effective cost is $118,816.94, or 79.2 percent of the purchase price. Discounting matters more when the asset is long-lived and the discount rate is high. On the sale, the adjusted basis after two years is $150,000 minus $30,000 minus $48,000, which is $72,000, so the gain is $28,000. Because the asset is section 1245 property, that gain is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken, taxed at 25 percent rather than at a capital rate, which is $7,000. The learner who treats recapture as a capital gain understates the tax and overstates the net proceeds.

questions.prompt: A pension promises GBP 18,000 a year for 20 years, indexed at 2.5 percent, with the first payment one year from now. Compute its present value at a 5 percent discount rate, the value of the same promise with no indexation, and the discount rate implied by a transfer value of GBP 260,000.
questions.answer: The indexed promise is worth GBP 275,344.34, the level promise GBP 224,319.79, and a transfer value of GBP 260,000 implies a discount rate of about 5.63 percent, which is above the 5 percent used to value the promise
questions.distractor: The promise is worth GBP 360,000 because 18,000 a year for 20 years is 360,000, so a transfer value of 260,000 is poor by 100,000 and should be refused on that basis
questions.correction: Adding 20 payments without discounting values a stream of money in today's terms only if the discount rate is zero. At 5 percent, 18,000 a year for 20 years is worth 224,319.79, and indexation at 2.5 percent raises that to 275,344.34 because each payment is larger than the last. The undiscounted 360,000 is not comparable to a transfer value quoted today, and the gap between 275,344 and 260,000 is 15,344, or 5.6 percent, not 100,000. The implied rate of 5.63 percent is the useful comparison: it says the transfer value is priced at a slightly higher discount rate than the 5 percent assumption, so it is modestly cheap rather than obviously bad. Mortality, guarantees and tax would still have to be priced before any decision.

questions.prompt: A UK estate is worth GBP 2,150,000 including a home of GBP 620,000 left to the deceased's children. The nil-rate band is GBP 325,000, the residence nil-rate band is GBP 175,000, and the residence band tapers by GBP 1 for every GBP 2 of estate above GBP 2,000,000. Compute the tax at 40 percent and the effective rate.
questions.answer: The residence band is reduced by GBP 75,000 to GBP 100,000, so the allowance is GBP 425,000, the taxable estate is GBP 1,725,000, the tax is GBP 690,000 and the effective rate is 32.09 percent
questions.distractor: The allowance is GBP 500,000 because the home passes to direct descendants, so the taxable estate is GBP 1,650,000 and the tax is GBP 660,000
questions.correction: The residence band is not a fixed GBP 175,000 once the estate exceeds GBP 2,000,000. The excess here is GBP 150,000, so the band falls by GBP 75,000 to GBP 100,000 and the total allowance is GBP 425,000. Tax is 40 percent of GBP 1,725,000, which is GBP 690,000, an effective rate of 32.09 percent rather than the 30.7 percent the distractor produces. The taper also creates a marginal rate above 40 percent: within the taper zone each extra GBP 1,000 of estate adds GBP 500 to the taxable amount through the lost band and GBP 400 of tax on the GBP 1,000 itself, so the marginal rate is 60 percent until the band is exhausted at GBP 2,350,000.

questions.prompt: A firm has EBITDA of $900,000 and four committed annual charges: mortgage payments of $27,600, an equipment lease of $29,460, an indexed services contract starting at $600,000 with a 4 percent annual cap, and pension contributions of $60,000. Compute the coverage ratio in year one, then in year five when the contract has escalated three times.
questions.answer: Year one charges are $717,060, so coverage is 1.26 times, and in year five the contract reaches $701,915.14, charges reach $818,975.14 and coverage falls to 1.10 times, which is a 12 percent reduction in cover from escalation alone
questions.distractor: Coverage is 1.26 times and stays there, because the contract is capped at 4 percent and a cap protects the firm from the cost of escalation
questions.correction: A cap limits each annual increase; it does not stop the increases compounding. At 4 percent a year the contract rises from $600,000 to $701,915.14 by year five, which adds $101,915.14 of annual charges and cuts coverage from 1.26 to 1.10 even though nothing else changed. The cap did work: at an uncapped 5.5 percent the year-five charge would be $743,000 and coverage would be about 1.06. But the register should show the capped path as a forecast rather than treating the cap as a guarantee of constant cover. The same error appears whenever a fixed cap is read as a fixed cost.

questions.prompt: A loan of $315,000 at 6.90 percent over 240 months has a payment of $2,423.32. The borrower is offered 5.95 percent over a fresh 240 months with closing costs of $5,200 and a 1 percent prepayment penalty. Compute the new payment, the monthly saving, the break-even and the interest saved over the term.
questions.answer: The penalty is $3,150 and the new balance $323,350, so the payment is $2,307.26, the saving is $116.06 a month, the break-even is 71.9 months, and interest falls from $266,596.70 to $230,392.97, a saving of $36,203.73
questions.distractor: The payment is $2,307.26 and the saving is $116.06, so the break-even is 71.9 months and the deal is worth doing because a 0.95 point rate cut on $315,000 saves about $2,993 a year
questions.correction: The arithmetic on the payment is right and the annual-saving shortcut is not. A 0.95 point cut on $315,000 is $2,993 a year only if the balance stayed at $315,000 for the whole year, which it does not; the actual saving is $116.06 times 12, or $1,392.72 a year, against $8,350 of upfront cost. The break-even of 71.9 months is the correct test, and it is satisfied here because the term is 240 months, unlike the case where the term is short and the break-even exceeds it. The interest saving of $36,203.73 is real but arrives gradually, so the break-even, not the total interest figure, is what determines whether the borrower is better off if they move or repay early.

questions.prompt: A 5/1 adjustable-rate mortgage of $425,000 at 6.10 percent over 360 months has a payment of $2,575.48 and a balance of $395,966.62 after five years. The margin is 2.60 percent, the index at the first reset is 4.30 percent, and the caps are 2/2/6. Compute the reset rate and the new payment.
questions.answer: The fully indexed rate is 6.90 percent, which is within the 2 point initial cap, so the payment becomes $2,773.40, an increase of $197.92 or 7.68 percent
questions.distractor: The rate resets to 8.10 percent because the margin is added to the start rate of 6.10 percent and then the index is added, so the payment rises by about $600
questions.correction: The margin is added to the index, not to the previous rate: 4.30 plus 2.60 is 6.90 percent. Adding the margin to the note rate as well double counts the lender's spread and produces 8.70 percent before the index is applied; following that path, the initial cap would cut the rate to 8.10 percent and the payment would be $3,082.41. The correct calculation amortises $395,966.62 over the remaining 300 months at 6.90 percent, which gives $2,773.40. Because the original payment of $2,575.48 was already amortising the same balance over 300 months at 6.10 percent, the increase is modest at 7.68 percent. Note also that the lifetime cap of 6 points above the start rate sets a maximum of 12.10 percent, so the household's worst case is bounded but far above today's payment.

questions.prompt: A machine costing $90,000 can be leased for 60 payments of $1,830 or bought with a 60-month loan at 7.75 percent, which costs $1,814.13 a month. Compute the implicit rate in the lease, the total payments under each option, and the difference.
questions.answer: The lease payments discount to $90,000 at 8.12 percent, which is 0.37 points above the 7.75 percent loan, and the lease costs $109,800 against $108,847.58, so the lease is $952.42 more expensive
questions.distractor: The lease carries an implicit rate of 7.75 percent because that is the market rate for the asset, so the two options are equivalent apart from $952.42 of rounding
questions.correction: The implicit rate is not the market rate; it is the rate that equates 60 payments of $1,830 to $90,000 today, and it is 8.12 percent. The $952.42 difference is not rounding, it is the price of the 0.37 point spread, and on a larger asset or a longer term the same spread grows. Dividing total payments by the number of months would give an average payment but no rate, and it cannot handle a residual value or a lease with an initial payment. The method that works is to solve for the discount rate, then compare it with the borrower's marginal cost of borrowing, which is the 7.75 percent loan here.

questions.prompt: A UK exporter invoices EUR 600,000 with payment in 180 days. Spot is 1.0855 dollars per euro and the 180-day forward is 1.0800. Compute the cost of the forward against spot in dollars and as an annualised percentage, then state the unhedged receipt if spot is 1.0600 at payment.
questions.answer: The forward locks $648,000 against $651,300 at spot, a cost of $3,300 or 0.51 percent over 180 days, which annualises to about 1.03 percent, and at 1.0600 the unhedged receipt is $636,000, which is $12,000 below the forward
questions.distractor: The forward costs 0.55 cents per euro, so the annualised cost is 0.55 percent and the exporter should stay unhedged because a half percent fee is pure loss
questions.correction: The 0.0055 difference is dollars per euro, and as a proportion of 1.0855 it is 0.51 percent for 180 days, which annualises by 365 over 180 to 1.03 percent. Calling that 0.55 percent a year understates the cost by about half. The second error is treating the forward cost as a fee with no benefit: at 1.0600 the exporter receives $636,000 unhedged, so the forward is worth $12,000 relative to that outcome. Whether cover is worth 1.03 percent a year depends on the firm's margin and on whether a 2.3 percent currency move would breach a covenant, which is why the cost should be compared with the size of the exposure rather than dismissed as a fee.

questions.prompt: A director guarantees 100 percent of a $300,000 facility. The lender estimates a 5 percent annual default probability and 40 percent recovery. Compute the expected annual loss and state what the guarantee does to the director's other borrowing if the facility is called at 8 percent interest-only.
questions.answer: Expected loss is $300,000 times 0.05 times 0.60, which is $9,000 a year, and a call would add $24,000 of annual interest to the director's personal cash flow, so a lender assessing the director's next loan would treat $300,000 as a contingent exposure
questions.distractor: Expected loss is $15,000 because 5 percent of $300,000 is $15,000, and the guarantee is only a disclosure item because the company is expected to repay
questions.correction: The 40 percent recovery belongs in the calculation: the loss given default is 60 percent of the balance, so the expected loss is $9,000 rather than $15,000. Understating or overstating the expected loss is a secondary matter, however, because the guarantee's main effect is on capacity. In the bad state the director owes $24,000 a year of interest at 8 percent, and a lender will count the full $300,000 as a contingent liability when computing debt service, which can remove borrowing capacity entirely. The expected loss is a pricing number; the exposure is a balance-sheet constraint, and conflating them is the error.

questions.prompt: A four-year supply contract starts at GBP 360,000 a year with a 3.5 percent annual cap and no floor. CPI runs at 4.5 percent each year. Compute the annual charges and the total over four years.
questions.answer: The cap binds every year, so the charges are GBP 360,000, 372,600, 385,641 and 399,138, a total of GBP 1,517,379, which is GBP 77,379 above four years at the base charge
questions.distractor: The charges rise by 4.5 percent a year because the cap only applies if the index exceeds 5 percent, giving a total of about GBP 1,539,000
questions.correction: The cap applies whenever CPI exceeds 3.5 percent, which it does at 4.5 percent, so each increase is 3.5 percent and not 4.5 percent. The charges compound at 1.035, giving 399,138 in year four and a four-year total of 1,517,379. The difference from the uncapped path is the value of the cap to the buyer: at 4.5 percent the four-year total would be 1,538,470, so the cap saves about 21,091. Do not read the cap as a fixed increase, either: 3.5 percent compounding still adds 10.9 percent to the charge over three reviews, and that is the number to test against the margin.

questions.prompt: A firm buys equipment for $240,000, depreciates it as five-year MACRS property with the half-year convention, and pays tax at 26 percent. Compute the six annual deductions, the present value of the tax shield at 9 percent, and the tax on a sale for $70,000 after four years.
questions.answer: Deductions are $48,000, $76,800, $46,080, $27,648, $27,648 and $13,824, the shield is worth $49,415.23 at 9 percent, and a sale at $70,000 after four years gives a $28,528 gain on a $41,472 basis, taxed at 26 percent for $7,417.28
questions.distractor: The shield is worth $62,400 because 26 percent of $240,000 is $62,400, and the sale is a capital gain of $70,000 minus $28,528 of remaining basis, taxed at the capital rate
questions.correction: The $62,400 is the undiscounted total of a 26 percent deduction on the full cost, and the deductions are spread over six tax years, so the present value at 9 percent is $49,415.23. The 9 percent rate matters: at 4 percent the same shield would be worth more than $55,000, so quoting the undiscounted figure overstates the benefit of a long depreciation schedule. On the sale, the adjusted basis after four years is $240,000 minus $48,000, $76,800, $46,080 and $27,648, which is $41,472. The $28,528 gain is ordinary income to the extent of depreciation taken under section 1245, so the tax is $7,417.28 at 26 percent, not a capital rate.

questions.prompt: A pension promises GBP 30,000 a year for 25 years, indexed at 2 percent, with the first payment in one year. Compute the present value at a 4 percent discount rate, the value if the pension were level, and the rate implied by a transfer value of GBP 480,000.
questions.answer: The indexed promise is worth GBP 576,871.69, the level promise GBP 468,662.40, and the transfer value of GBP 480,000 implies a discount rate of about 5.66 percent, so the transfer is priced above the 4 percent used in the valuation
questions.distractor: The promise is worth GBP 750,000 because 30,000 a year for 25 years is 750,000, and the transfer value of 480,000 is therefore a loss of 270,000
questions.correction: The 750,000 is an undiscounted sum and cannot be compared with a transfer value quoted today; at 4 percent the level stream is worth 468,662.40 and indexation lifts it to 576,871.69. The transfer value of 480,000 is above the level value and below the indexed value, which is exactly why the implied rate is the right diagnostic: solving for the rate that equates the indexed payments to 480,000 gives 5.66 percent. That number can be compared with the return available on other assets and with the scheme's own funding assumptions. A difference of 96,872 between the 4 percent valuation and the quote is not a loss; it is the price of a different discount rate, and the decision turns on which rate is right rather than on the size of the gap.

questions.prompt: A UK estate is worth GBP 2,400,000, with the home passing to the children. The nil-rate band is GBP 325,000, the residence nil-rate band is GBP 175,000 and tapers by GBP 1 for every GBP 2 above GBP 2,000,000. Compute the tax and the effective rate, then compare it with a calculation that uses the full GBP 500,000 allowance.
questions.answer: The estate exceeds the taper threshold by GBP 400,000, so the residence band is reduced to nil, the taxable estate is GBP 2,075,000, the tax is GBP 830,000 and the effective rate is 34.58 percent, which is GBP 70,000 more than the GBP 760,000 produced by using the full allowance
questions.distractor: The allowance is GBP 500,000 because the home passes to direct descendants, so the tax is GBP 760,000 and the effective rate is 31.67 percent
questions.correction: The residence band is fully withdrawn at GBP 2,400,000: the excess over GBP 2,000,000 is GBP 400,000, so the reduction is GBP 200,000, which exceeds the GBP 175,000 band. Only the GBP 325,000 nil-rate band remains, giving tax of 40 percent on GBP 2,075,000, which is GBP 830,000. Using the full allowance understates the tax by GBP 70,000, a 9.2 percent error, and the error grows with the estate until the band is gone. The taper is also why the effective rate rises steeply between GBP 2,000,000 and GBP 2,350,000 rather than staying at 40 percent of the excess.

questions.prompt: A firm lists four commitments: a $400,000 loan at 6.50 percent over 120 months with payments of $4,541.92, a 60-month equipment lease at $2,455 a month, an indexed services contract of $480,000 a year for five years with 4 percent annual escalation, and a guarantee with a 10 percent chance of a $200,000 call in year three. Discount everything at 6 percent and rank the commitments by present value.
questions.answer: The contract is worth $2,180,308.20 of present value, the loan $409,106.42, the lease $126,986.25 and the guarantee $16,792.39, so the indexed contract is 79.8 percent of the $2,733,193.26 total and dwarfs every credit commitment on the register
questions.distractor: The contract costs $480,000 a year, the loan $54,503, the lease $29,460 and the guarantee nothing until it is called, so the loan and lease are the commitments that matter and the contract is merely an operating expense
questions.correction: Ranking by year-one cash flow treats a contract that runs for five years and escalates as if it were a single year of spending, and it treats a contingent guarantee as zero. On a present value basis at 6 percent the contract is $2,180,308.20, more than five times the loan and lease combined, because it is the largest annual amount and it runs for five years. The guarantee is small in expected value at $16,792.39 and large in consequence, since a call is a $200,000 lump sum. Different commitments need different measures: present value ranks the ordinary streams, expected loss prices the contingency, and the cash call sizes the tail. A register that uses one measure for all four hides the two that matter most.

questions.prompt: A firm borrows $400,000 at 6.50 percent over 120 months, paying $4,541.92 a month, and separately signs a three-year services contract with an exit fee of $45,000. In month 24 it wants to exit both. The loan carries a 3 percent prepayment penalty in the first two years and the balance is $339,297.79. Compute the total cost of exit and the payments avoided.
questions.answer: The penalty is $10,178.93 and the exit fee is $45,000, so exit costs $55,178.93, while the 96 remaining payments of $4,541.92 total $436,024.23
questions.distractor: Exit costs $45,000 because the prepayment penalty only applies when a loan is repaid in full in the first year, and the remaining payments of $436,024.23 are avoided in full
questions.correction: The penalty applies to a full repayment inside the window stated in the contract, and month 24 sits inside a three-year window, so 3 percent of the $339,297.79 balance is owed in addition to the services exit fee. The total of $55,178.93 is the number to compare with the value of exiting, not the $45,000 alone. The 96 remaining payments of $4,541.92 total $436,024.23, but avoiding them is not a saving of that amount, because the firm also gives up whatever the asset or service was producing. The correct comparison is the present value of the remaining payments plus the exit costs against the present value of the benefits lost, and the penalty is the part of that comparison most often left out.

questions.prompt: A firm has a EUR 800,000 receivable due in 90 days at a spot rate of 1.0750 and a personal guarantee of $250,000 with a 4 percent default probability and 30 percent recovery. The euro falls to 1.0300 and the guarantee is called at 8 percent interest-only. Compute the currency loss, the expected loss on the guarantee and the annual cash cost of a call.
questions.answer: The receivable falls from $860,000 to $824,000, a loss of $36,000, the guarantee has an expected loss of $7,000, and a call adds $20,000 a year of interest, so the two events together put $56,000 of annual cash at risk
questions.distractor: The currency loss is $36,000, the guarantee loss is $10,000 because 4 percent of $250,000 is $10,000, and the total exposure is therefore $46,000
questions.correction: The guarantee loss must use the loss given default: 70 percent of $250,000 is the exposure that is not recovered, so 4 percent of $175,000 is $7,000, not $10,000. The larger correction is about what to add up. The $36,000 currency loss is a realised reduction in receipts, while the guarantee contributes $7,000 of expected loss and $20,000 a year of interest if called, so summing expected loss and realised loss into a single figure mixes a probability-weighted number with a definite one. A commitment register keeps them apart: realised items change this year's cash, expected losses price the contingency, and the called guarantee changes next year's fixed charges.
